Title: Enhancing Higher-Order Cognitive Abilities Through AI-Powered Smart Assistants: Implications for Digital Entrepreneurship and Future Problem-Solving in Higher Education
Source title: Journal of Intelligence
Abstract: Higher education is undergoing a rapid transformation driven by advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), creating new opportunities to support the development of higher-order cognitive skills through carefully designed learning environments. This study aimed to examine the effectiveness of an educational program that integrates AI-powered intelligent assistants into a structured e-learning environment to support the development of digital entrepreneurship and future-oriented problem-solving skills among graduate students. A quasi-experimental design was used with 82 graduate students, randomly assigned to two groups: an experimental group (n = 41) and a control group (n = 41). Both groups studied the same educational content and completed identical learning activities; however, the experimental group participated in a structured learning framework that included AI-powered intelligent assistants, guided learning activities, and instructor facilitation, while the control group completed the same activities without AI support. The educational program comprised five modules focusing on chatbot design, intelligent platform development, digital content production, educational data analysis, and future-oriented problem-solving. Learning outcomes were assessed using a Digital Entrepreneurship Product Rating Scale and a Future-Oriented Problem-Solving Scale, which measures skills in visualization, prediction, foresight, and planning. The results revealed statistically significant differences favoring the experimental group on both outcome scales, with large effect sizes. These findings suggest that integrating AI-powered intelligent assistants within a structured learning framework may support the development of digital entrepreneurship and future-oriented problem-solving skills among graduate students. This study contributes empirical evidence to the potential educational value of integrating AI-powered intelligent assistants with pedagogically designed learning activities to foster higher-level cognitive development in higher education. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Large Language Models for simplifying directly-follows graphs in support of self-regulated learning
Source title: Computers in Human Behavior Reports
Abstract: Directly-Follows Graphs (DFGs) derived from educational process mining provide rich evidence of students’ interaction patterns in virtual learning environments, but their complexity often hinders interpretation by instructors and researchers. This study investigates how Large Language Models (LLMs) can support learning analytics by transforming complex DFGs into simplified models and interpretable summaries of student behaviour, with a specific focus on self-regulated learning (SRL). We analyse the actual event log of a compulsory undergraduate course in a Computer Science degree (87 students, ∼140k events), discovering a DFG using PM4Py, and compare several GPT-5 variants and reasoning configurations for the task of simplifying this model. The LLM is prompted to remove less relevant transitions while preserving core behaviour. We examine the structural impact of simplification and qualitatively analyse behavioural patterns in a representative simplified DFG. Results reveal a spectrum of trade-offs: smaller models tend to over-prune, whereas larger ones produce more conservative reductions with higher coverage. Despite substantial simplification, the selected GPT-5 configuration preserves navigation, assessment and grade-monitoring patterns that can be interpreted in terms of planning, performance and reflection phases of SRL. We argue that such human-readable process summaries can help instructors detect less effective behaviours, redesign course workflows and scaffold SRL, positioning LLM-assisted DFG simplification as a promising bridge between algorithmic process mining and educational decision-making. © 2026 The Authors.

Authors: Yuan B.; You S.
Title: Coffee-Mate: Assisting keyframe selection via self-distillation for video question answering
Source title: Pattern Recognition
Abstract: Video question answering (VideoQA) aims to infer precise answers from given question-video pairs. Existing methods utilize uniformly sampled frames and keyframe selection in continuous frames, where uniform sampling easily misses the critical question-relevant visual cues. Though keyframe selection methods can screen out question-critical frames, they (1) lack of supervision for essential keyframes, relying on fixed frame selection modules or attention scores between frames and questions, which prevent the model from receiving feedback to improve keyframe selection, and (2) overlook the importance of maintaining comprehensive temporal coverage, struggling with causal and temporal reasoning due to incomplete temporal information. To this end, we propose Coffee-Mate (CoMa), assisting keyframe selection via self-distillation for VideoQA. Firstly, we introduce a more-to-less self-distillation strategy, where a student model with selected keyframe inputs (less) distills knowledge from a teacher model with unfiltered frame inputs (more). The teacher's richer and more complete temporal context acts as self-supervised guidance, ensuring the retention of critical frames for coherent event narratives. Secondly, we introduce multi-level distillation loss to encourage the student model to inherit the question-relevant understanding from the teacher model. Thirdly, we propose segmented frame selection to obtain the most relevant frames, which re-uses the teacher model to select the question-relevant and comprehensive temporal-related frames. Extensive experiments on 6 benchmark datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the more-to-less self-distillation method achieves considerable improvements even without frame selection, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving video comprehension. Title: Human-in-the-Loop AI Feedback in Interpreter Training: An ASR-Based Platform Analysis of Instructor Annotations, Comment Functions, and System Constraints
Source title: Applied Sciences (Switzerland)
Abstract: The use of AI-assisted feedback systems has steadily increased in higher education, yet there has been limited research as to which components of expert feedback can be supported by AI and which require continued human judgment. This issue is particularly important in professional training domains where feedback must rely upon contextual interpretation, source–output comparison, and domain expertise. Accordingly, this study analyzes instructor-generated feedback in TalkTrack, an automatic speech recognition (ASR)-supported digital platform for interpreter training, as a basis for human-in-the-loop AI feedback design. The dataset consists of 44 Korean–Japanese, Japanese–Korean, and Chinese–Korean interpreting performances produced by 12 graduate students and includes 931 feedback tags and 756 substantive qualitative comments manually assigned by 10 instructors. The categories most frequently assigned were expression and translation-error feedback, while corrective feedback was the dominant instructional function. Further, feedback behavior varied substantially by instructor and feedback category, indicating that different types of feedback require different levels of human intervention and system support. Accordingly, this study proposes a human-in-the-loop feedback architecture employing ASR and large language models to support detection, organization, retrieval, and suggestion generation, while instructors retain responsibility for source-text fidelity, discourse coherence, pedagogical judgment, and final feedback validation, from which this study proposes empirical design requirements for scalable AI-supported feedback systems in professional e-learning environments. © 2026 by the author.

Title: Mapping Artificial Intelligence–Supported Community of Inquiry Research in Higher Education: A Scientometric Analysis Using CiteSpace
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping collaborative inquiry in higher education, yet its integration with the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework remains conceptually and methodologically fragmented. This study employs CiteSpace-based scientometric analysis to map the intellectual structure, thematic evolution, and emerging trends of AI-supported CoI research. A curated dataset of 85 publications from Web of Science and Scopus was analyzed through reference co-citation, keyword co-occurrence, and citation burst detection. Results indicate that the field remains anchored in CoI’s core constructs (cognitive and social presence and related component dimensions), while AI functions primarily as an enabling analytic and design layer. Emerging fronts such as learning analytics, machine learning, and generative AI suggest a trajectory from theory building to data-driven expansion and, more recently, AI-supported learning design and discourse analysis. Burst detection further highlights growing attention to engagement, online discussion, and AI-enhanced collaboration, underscoring the hybrid evolution of pedagogical theory and computational methods. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: He K.; Wu J.; Wang C.
Title: Dynamic knowledge landscape construction for AI-driven emergency decision-making: An STM-LLM framework with triple-LLM synergistic labeling
Source title: Information Processing and Management
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance emergency decision-making, but systematic reviews of its knowledge evolution remain lacking. Based on 525 papers on AI-driven emergency decision-making (AI-EDM) from Web of Science (2020–2025), this study proposes an STM-LLM framework integrating Structural Topic Modeling (STM) and Large Language Models (LLMs), and develops a Triple-LLM Synergistic Labeling (TLS) mechanism for automated and bias-resistant topic labeling generation. To validate the efficacy of the framework, systematic comparative and ablation experiments were designed. The application of the framework in the field of AI-EDM facilitates the identification of research topics, followed by analysis of their spatiotemporal distribution and evolution. A Logistic-Normal Generalized Linear Model (GLM) quantified the effects of five covariates on topic prevalence, and a three-dimensional strategic map identified research frontiers and gaps. The experimental results show that the STM-LLM framework significantly outperforms mainstream baseline methods in both topic label quality and generation efficiency, and the TLS mechanism effectively improves labeling stability. The study identified nine stable topics in the AI-EDM domain that show a “growth-consolidation-decline” pattern. Research funding showed a positive correlation with the development of human–AI collaborative platforms ((Formula presented) ), and differences in research focus were observed between Chinese and international scholars. None of the topics demonstrated significant preferences in terms of collaboration type. Both human intervention and type of decision objective demonstrated distinct patterns of association with different topics. Furthermore, Topics are categorized into four types—Leading, Emerging, Receding, and Persistent. Based on these findings, we further propose a “problem–technology–benefit” framework to systematically support domain advancement. The STM-LLM framework automates dynamic knowledge landscape construction, overcoming manual topic labeling limitations and offering data-driven methodological and practical support for AI-EDM research. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: PG-LLM-KT: An adaptable prerequisite-guided framework for knowledge tracing with frozen lightweight LLMs
Source title: Knowledge-Based Systems
Abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) seeks to model students’ evolving knowledge state from historical learning interactions. However, deep learning-based methods show limited generalizability, LLM-based methods exhibit high computational cost, and graph-enhanced methods depend on externally predefined graphs. To address these issues, we propose PG-LLM-KT, an adaptable graph-guided KT framework supporting frozen lightweight LLMs. Firstly, PG-LLM-KT constructs a data-driven prerequisite knowledge graph from student interaction sequences to capture temporal and conditional concept dependencies. Then, it incorporates the graph into a structured instruction template to guide LLM reasoning in accordance with dataset-specific knowledge structures. To address overconfidence common in lightweight LLMs, an adaptive confidence head is introduced to adjust prediction confidence. Extensive experiments across diverse KT datasets, including a self-built dataset HNU_SYS2023, show that PG-LLM-KT achieves competitive performance, while maintaining high computational efficiency and strong cross-dataset generalization, offering an interpretable and scalable KT solution for real-world educational applications. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Abstract: The learning states of students in class, online and blended learning are difficult to determine from a single source of data due to the discontinuous nature of observations and fluctuations in the quality of videos/texts. Title: Explaining ChatGPT Adoption in Higher Education: Insights for AI Literacy, Educational Practice, and Responsible AI
Source title: Education Sciences
Abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence tools, particularly ChatGPT, is transforming teaching and learning in higher education. This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) framework that integrates the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT2), machine learning, and explainability techniques to examine students’ intentions to use ChatGPT in academic contexts. Survey data were analyzed using Ordinary Least Squares regression, Random Forest, SHAP, Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), Importance–Performance Map Analysis (IPMA), and K-Means clustering. The results indicate that Habit, Performance Expectancy, Hedonic Motivation, Social Influence, and Facilitating Conditions significantly influence behavioral intention, explaining 67.6% of the variance. Habit emerged as the strongest predictor, whereas Price Value had negligible influence. XAI analyses revealed that Effort Expectancy acts as a necessary condition for high adoption levels despite its limited direct effect. Four distinct student profiles were identified, highlighting heterogeneous patterns of AI integration and informing strategies for responsible and effective educational adoption. These findings provide evidence-based guidance for integrating AI literacy, responsible AI practices, and pedagogically meaningful ChatGPT use in higher education curricula. © 2026 by the authors.

Authors: Park J.; Lim H.-W.
Title: Self-Regulated ChatGPT Use in Elementary EFL Writing: A Multiple Case Study
Source title: Journal of Asia TEFL
Abstract: This study examined how Korean elementary EFL learners engaged in self-regulated use of ChatGPT during AI-assisted writing, focusing on prompting practices, feedback uptake, and reflective evaluation across successive writing tasks. Adopting a multiple case design, the study involved four sixth-grade Korean EFL learners. Data comprised learner-ChatGPT interaction logs, structured self-reports, post-session interviews, initial and revised drafts, and a post-study interview. The findings revealed consistent directional shifts across all three analytical dimensions. Regarding prompting, participants progressively moved away from direct text generation requests toward more dialogic, evaluative, and guidance-oriented strategies. Regarding feedback uptake, participants increasingly evaluated ChatGPT suggestions against their own communicative intentions and linguistic intuitions, selectively incorporating or rejecting feedback. Regarding reflective evaluation, participants demonstrated growing awareness of how to regulate their ChatGPT interactions and selectively incorporate its feedback. Notably, evaluative awareness alone did not uniformly enable strategic use; linguistic knowledge and learner agency appeared as moderating factors. The findings suggest that elementary-level EFL learners are capable of developing self-regulated and strategic orientations toward ChatGPT, repositioning it from a text provider to an interactive resource supporting their own writing decisions. Sustained instructional scaffolding targeting linguistic confidence and learner agency is recommended to support self-regulated AI use in L2 writing. www.earticle.net. © 2004 AsiaTEFL.org. Title: Simulating Neurodiverse Communication Patterns in Large Language Models
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in educational, clinical, and communicative settings, yet their ability to simulate neurodiverse communication styles remains insufficiently examined. Existing work has focused mainly on adapting AI to support neurodivergent users, rather than modelling neurodivergent communication as a meaningful and informative behavioural pattern. This study presents an exploratory qualitative validation, examining whether LLMs can simulate recognisable communication traits associated with Attention-Deficit/ Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) and Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD), with the aim of supporting empathy-building and professional training rather than diagnosis or intervention. This work does not aim to improve behavioural realism, but to systematically examine what current LLM architectures can and cannot represent. A controlled classroom interaction was used, in which two language models adopted teacher and student roles, with the student model configured to display neurodivergent traits through structured prompt engineering. Three prompt engineering approaches were tested: general trait guidance, explicit trait definitions with severity levels, and program-assisted probabilistic variation. Outputs were evaluated by experts in artificial intelligence and speech and language therapy for trait recognisability, educational value, and ethical considerations. Findings suggest that LLMs can consistently represent certain traits, particularly ADHD-related behaviours such as impulsivity and topic shifting. However, the models struggled to reflect interactional tension, emotional regulation, and nonverbal or sensory aspects, especially in autistic profiles. These results demonstrate both the instructional potential and the inherent limits of text-based simulation, underscoring that such models should be used as illustrative tools rather than representations of lived neurodivergent experience. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Single-Agent vs. Multi-agents for Automated Video Analysis of On-Screen Collaborative Learning Behaviors
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: On-screen learning behavior provides valuable insights into how students seek, use, and create information during learning. Analyzing on-screen behavioral engagement is essential for capturing students’ cognitive and collaborative processes. The recent development of Vision Language Models (VLMs) offers new opportunities to automate the labor-intensive manual coding often required for multimodal video data analysis. In this study, we compared the performance of both leading closed-source VLMs (Claude-3.7-Sonnet, GPT-4.1) and open-source VLM (Qwen2.5-VL-72B) in single- and multi-agent settings for automated coding of screen recordings in collaborative learning contexts based on the ICAP framework. In particular, we proposed and compared two multi-agent frameworks: 1) a three-agent workflow multi-agent system (MAS) that segments screen videos by scene and detects on-screen behaviors using cursor-informed VLM prompting with evidence-based verification; 2) an autonomous-decision MAS inspired by ReAct that iteratively interleaves reasoning, tool-like operations (segmentation/ classification/ validation), and observation-driven self-correction to produce interpretable on-screen behavior labels. Experimental results demonstrated that the two proposed MAS frameworks achieved viable performance, outperforming the single VLMs in scene and action detection tasks. It is worth noting that the workflow-based agent achieved best on scene detection, and the autonomous-decision MAS achieved best on action detection. This study demonstrates the effectiveness of VLM-based Multi-agent System for video analysis and contributes a scalable framework for multimodal data analytics. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Metacognitive Filtering and Cognitive Offloading in AI-Assisted L2 Writing: A PRISMA Guided Process-Tracing Synthesis
Source title: Behavioral Sciences
Abstract: This study conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 33 empirical studies examining learner interactions with AI-mediated feedback in L2 writing between 2010 and 2025. Evidence was synthesized from process-tracing methods, including keystroke logging, eye-tracking, screen capture, interaction logs, and draft-history analytics. The findings revealed two recurring interaction profiles. Higher-regulation learners typically engaged in selective uptake, recursive evaluation, and extended processing of AI feedback, whereas lower-regulation learners more frequently indicate rapid acceptance and reduced evaluative engagement. Across studies, micro-level feedback was associated with shorter revision latencies and burst-editing patterns, whereas macro-level feedback was associated with longer processing times and repeated revision cycles. The review also identified substantial methodological variability in trace precision, AI transparency, multimodal triangulation, and reproducibility practices. Overall, the evidence suggests that the effectiveness of AI-mediated feedback depends not only on the quality of the feedback provided but also on how learners regulate and engage with it during revision. Greater methodological transparency and more rigorous process-tracing designs are needed to strengthen future research on AI-supported writing development. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: An Exploratory Pilot for Leveraging Generative AI to Extract Non-Technical Skills from Audio in Medical Crisis Resource Management Scenarios
Source title: Applied Sciences (Switzerland)
Abstract: The assessment of non-technical skills (NTSs) is a key task in the medical field. However, it is difficult to implement because it relies on experts assessing trainees. This is a time-consuming process that can differ between evaluators. In recent decades, NTS rating scales have been developed to reduce subjectivity in crisis resource management (CRM) scenarios. Additionally, many tools have been developed to automatically measure NTSs. However, these objective automated tools calculate low-level metrics that are sometimes difficult to correlate with NTS behaviors. Leadership metrics, for example, have rarely been explored in the existing literature, nor have speech content metrics. This work proposes a cost-effective pilot solution for extracting and visualizing NTS behaviors from CRM audio content. The exploratory pipeline consists of three independent steps, each of which was evaluated for the feasibility of automation: (1) pre-processing the audio and creating transcrips via automatic speech-to-text conversion; (2) using a generative artificial intelligence large language model to collect structured data on communication interactions and NTSs from the transcripts; and (3) formatting the data to provide insightful visualizations of the CRM scenario. The results of the first phase showed that WhisperX performed best at generating audio transcripts, and that some NR techniques improved transcript quality. However, there is still room for improvement regarding acknowledgments (ACKs) and speaker recognition. Preliminary results from the second phase showed that the developed NTS data model can extract relevant information from transcripts in a structured way. Nonetheless, the proposed prompts require refinement to infer data more accurately and improve order and NTS extraction results. Finally, the results of the third phase showed that the proposed knowledge graph visualizations effectively summarize what happened during the standardized scenario. This could enable evaluators to provide additional information during the debriefing session after the experience. This exploratory work contributes to the streamlining of NTS extraction during the evaluation process in standardized scenarios by proposing a pilot for NTS extraction and visualization from speech content. Further research is needed to optimize audio quality, refine the LLM prompts and achieve full automation of the pipeline. © 2026 by the authors.

Title: Hallucination Detection in Natural Language Generation via Knowledge-Transfer Distillation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: In Natural Language Generation (NLG), hallucinations occur when the models’ output content is semantically unsupported or factually incorrect, creating real serious challenges and critical problems for many real-world applications. In this research work, a novel framework for hallucination detection is proposed. Our method integrates the principles of knowledge transfer and knowledge distillation by utilizing the hard labels from a pre-trained NLI transformer model with soft probabilistic labels from a large teacher model (GPT-OSS-120B). We introduce a novel hybrid dual-objective loss function, termed Focal–Distillation Loss, which combines a modified Cross-Entropy—Focal Cross-Entropy—for hard labels with Kullback–Leibler divergence for soft probabilistic labels. This loss function is used to fine-tune the DeBERTa-v3 base model as the student model. This dual supervision with the new dual-objective loss enables the student model to capture complex patterns in the generated text and learn them. Our novel framework is demonstrated by an experiment on the SHROOM 2024 hallucination detection dataset, which achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an accuracy of 70.0% and outperforming several existing systems, and there is still room for improvement. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of combining model-based knowledge transfer with LLM-based distillation, supported by the proposed Focal–Distillation Loss, in advancing hallucination detection within Natural Language Generation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Honey, I Shrunk the Language Model: Impact of Knowledge Distillation Methods on Performance and Explainability
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
Abstract: AI has increasingly influenced modern society, recently in particular through significant advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, high computational and storage demands of LLMs still limit their deployment in resource-constrained environments. Knowledge distillation addresses this challenge by training a small student model from a larger teacher model. Previous research has introduced several distillation methods for both generating training data and training the student model. Despite their relevance, the effects of state-of-the-art distillation methods on model performance and explainability have not been thoroughly investigated and compared. In this work, we enlarge the set of available methods by applying critique-revision prompting to distillation for data generation and by synthesizing existing training methods. We systematically compare the distillation methods on the widely used Commonsense Question-Answering (CQA), Extended Stanford Natural Language Inference (ESNLI), and StrategyQA datasets. While we measure performance via student model accuracy, we employ a human-grounded study to evaluate explainability. We contribute new distillation methods and their comparison in terms of both performance and explainability. This should further advance the distillation of small language models and, thus, contribute to broader applicability and faster diffusion of language models. © 1989-2012 IEEE.

Title: Mapping neural network research in education through bibliometric analysis
Source title: Discover Education
Abstract: Neural networks are reshaping educational research and practice; yet evidence syntheses often treat them as part of a broader “AI in education” landscape, obscuring neural-network-specific trajectories, contributors, and themes. This study addresses that gap by providing a focused, methodologically transparent bibliometric mapping of neural network research in education. We analysed 704 Scopus-indexed journal articles published between 2010 and 2023, following PRISMA 2020 for identification, screening, and inclusion. Bibliometric performance analysis and science mapping were conducted using VOSviewer (for co-authorship, co-occurrence, and density visualisations) and the R-based Bibliometrix package (for descriptive indicators and thematic evolution). Network construction applied fractional counting and association-strength normalisation, with robustness checks using alternative thresholds. Findings show accelerated publication growth from 2019 onward, culminating in the highest output in 2023. The United States, the United Kingdom, and China lead productivity, while key institutions and author clusters function as collaboration hubs. Keyword co-occurrence reveals five dominant thematic clusters: (1) AI and machine learning foundations, (2) deep learning and neural network architectures, (3) learning analytics and personalised learning, (4) ethics, fairness, and explainability, and (5) higher education digital transformation. Thematic evolution indicates a shift from early automation-oriented work toward applied learning analytics and, more recently, governance concerns such as academic integrity and responsible AI, alongside emergent terms linked to generative AI. These results provide a replicable baseline for tracking intellectual structure, collaboration patterns, and ethical priorities in the field of neural network scholarship in education. We recommend strengthening interdisciplinary teams, expanding Global South participation through open infrastructure and partnerships, and prioritising transparent, fairness-aware designs when translating neural network research into educational policy and practice. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Presentism as a digital language ideology in generative AI discourse
Source title: Internet Pragmatics
Abstract: This paper gives a critical discourse-analytical account of presentism as a digital language ideology. It outlines how this ahistorical understanding of sociotechnical change centering the here-and-now as a site of disruption toward progress connects to enregistered forms of technological determinism. This becomes particularly relevant around digital language technologies including automation, algorithmic discourse and generative AI. This case study uses corpus-linguistic discourse analysis based on the NOW Corpus, as well as digital ethnography in the techno-optimist X community. By analyzing the syntactic constructions here to stay and will replace as discourse-syntactic indexicals of digital presentism, the study retraces how they contribute to larger ongoing discourses framing generative AI as inevitable and culturally progressive, both through the characterological figure of digital tech bros and their community of practice, and in digital journalistic discourse. Title: Evaluating LLM-Assisted CLO–PLO Alignment Decisions for AUN-QA–Aligned Curriculum Mapping
Source title: International Journal of Modern Education and Computer Science
Abstract: Curriculum mapping for AUN-QA is often time-consuming and prone to inconsistency because learning-outcome evidence is scattered across multiple courses and program documents. This study examines the reliability of large language models in supporting course learning outcome–program learning outcome (CLO–PLO) alignment decisions for AUN-QA–aligned curriculum mapping. Using Mechatronics Engineering curriculum materials (2022– 2024), AUN-QA v4.0 indicators were operationalized into a structured evidence schema to guide prompting and interpretation. GPT-4 produced 120 CLO–PLO alignment decisions, which were independently annotated by two domain experts and adjudicated by a third expert to establish reference labels. Model–reference agreement was evaluated using precision, recall, F1-score, and Cohen‘s kappa (κ) yielding 0.89, 0.85, 0.87, and 0.81, respectively. We also developed a dashboard that summarizes alignment coverage and supports PDCA-based curriculum improvement by flagging potential gaps and redundancies. Title: Language and Communication Students' Perceived Mastery in AI Chatbot Prompt Engineering: A Study on Vibe Coding in Educational Mobile Application Development
Source title: International Journal of Learning, Teaching and Educational Research
Abstract: This study examines language and communication students’ self-perceived mastery of AI chatbot prompt engineering, with particular attention to “vibe coding” for educational mobile application development. In this study, vibe coding refers to the deliberate use of prompts to shape tone, style, audience orientation, and user-facing educational content. Using a pattern-based framework centred on roles, constraints, and examples, the study investigates how students combine structure and exploratory prompting. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was administered online during March–July 2025 (Semester 2). Complete responses from 120 undergraduates were analysed from approximately 126 invited students (analytic response rate = 95.2%). The questionnaire demonstrated excellent overall internal consistency (Cronbach’s α = .965). Results indicate that students usually begin tasks with structured prompts but later move towards mixed or unstructured prompting styles, suggesting a control-then-explore sequence. Longer exposure to AI chatbots and more extensive prompt-engineering training were associated with higher self-perceived competency and output efficiency, whereas weekly usage frequency did not show statistically significant differences. Educational background was associated with prompting style and usage, but not with overall perceived competency or output efficiency, and gender differences were negligible. The findings suggest that scaffolded instruction in prompt engineering can support more confident and consistent student use of AI chatbots. Future research should triangulate self-reports with behavioural logs, archived prompts, and performance-based outputs. © The Authors.

Title: Supporting self-regulated learning through generative AI feedback in online higher education: the importance of student perceptions of the source of feedback
Source title: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
Abstract: Given the increased autonomy and limited direct instructor presence in online learning settings necessitating advanced self-regulated learning skills (SRLs), many online students face significant learning difficulties, such as low course completion rates. External support, particularly in the form of feedback, is crucial in addressing these difficulties. However, providing timely and personalised feedback at scale remains a key challenge. This study examines the effects of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) feedback on students' SRLs in an online higher education context. The study compares GenAI feedback, informed by student trace data and learning analytics, with tutor-generated feedback, assessing both student perceptions of feedback and their SRLs development. Employing a mixed-methods research design, we collected survey data, trace-based SRL indicators, and open-ended responses from 46 university students. Quantitative findings revealed that students rated GenAI feedback more positively than tutor-generated feedback, with a statistically significant difference in Genuineness. Moreover, the treatment group showed significant improvement in the Task Strategies dimension of SRLs, suggesting that personalised GenAI feedback may enhance specific regulatory behaviours. Qualitative insights revealed varying student awareness of the feedback source, with some prioritising content over the source of feedback. In contrast, others indicated their attitudes might have differed had they known the provider, highlighting the socio-emotional aspects of feedback adoption and impact. This study concludes that GenAI has the potential to scale SRLs feedback in online learning environments, but the student perceptions of feedback should be carefully managed to observe the expected impact. © The Author(s) 2026.

The decision layer combines decision trees and reinforcement learning to deliver interpretable yet adaptive interventions in dynamic environments. The execution layer outputs actionable recommendations for instructors, including pacing adjustment, tiered questioning, resource compensation, and after-class follow-up. A classroom-based evaluation was conducted in the Signal and Systems course for Class 2401-2 of the Electronic Information Science and Technology major at Wuhan Polytechnic University, involving 116 students. The aggregated results show that the proposed system improves the composite learning efficiency index, intervention hit rate, on-time assignment submission, quiz gain, and teacher diagnostic efficiency. Title: Turning hallucinations into knowledge: Towards identifying clickbait using LLM-generated fallacies
Source title: Information Processing and Management
Abstract: Knowledge hallucination, commonly known as LLM-generated responses that contain ”false or misleading information” presented as fact, has become one of the spotlight issues in current LLM-related studies, which could be ruinous for discriminative tasks, including clickbait detection. We then deploy a three-BERT-Encoders-embraced clickbait detection model that conducts contrastive learning for the inferences, as well as the semantic consistency learning between news and inferences. We additionally design a student model via knowledge distillation to avoid the influence of supervised inference production, thereby enabling the model testing to be inference-free. Our experiment results verified on three clickbait datasets demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms four kinds of baselines, including LLM prompting, SLM fine-tuning, and task-specific models across various metrics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Incorporating virtual reality in undergraduate internal medicine education: a scoping review of current evidence and implementation strategies
Source title: BMC Medical Education
Abstract: Background: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly recognized as a valuable tool in undergraduate medical education. It offers immersive, interactive environments that support experiential learning and skill development. However, its specific application in internal medicine education remains variably described. This scoping review aims to explore how VR is currently implemented in undergraduate internal medicine education, identify its educational outcomes, and highlight associated advantages, limitations, and gaps in literature. Methods: Following the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidelines, we conducted a comprehensive search of eight databases, including PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase. Studies were included if they addressed the use of VR in internal medicine education among undergraduate medical students. Data were extracted and analyzed thematically. Results: Of 1343 records screened, 9 studies published between 2017 and 2024 met the inclusion criteria. Studies originated from diverse countries and employed immersive and non-immersive VR technologies. Applications included teaching clinical reasoning, procedural skills, and emergency management. VR was associated with improved student engagement, satisfaction, and knowledge retention. Key advantages included scalability, safety, and cost-effectiveness. Limitations included technical challenges, limited physical interaction, and high initial costs. Few studies assessed long-term outcomes or included diverse, low-resource settings. Conclusion: VR is a promising adjunct to traditional internal medicine education, enhancing learner engagement and skill acquisition. However, its integration requires addressing technical barriers, ensuring faculty training, and expanding research to include diverse educational contexts and long-term effectiveness. © The Author(s) 2026.

Abstract: Student dropout prediction is regarded as one of the significant research fields in educational data mining. It aids the sustainability of institutions and early interventions in schools. The proposed framework combines heterogeneous base learner predictions with important original student-level features during meta-learning. As level-0 learners, Gradient Boosting, Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and Logistic Regression were adopted, whereas the meta-learner was Gradient Boosting. A synthetic educational dataset was used for the experimental assessment with 7,000 student records. The proposed eSDP framework achieved the highest overall predictive accuracy of all the models tested, with an F1-score of 0.928 and ROC-AUC of 0.987. Title: Sensitive Data Protection for Text-to-SQL Tasks in Large Language Models
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) dominate Text-to-SQL tasks thanks to strong language comprehension. Yet domain adaptation demands knowledge distillation and supervised fine-tuning, which usually rely on real business queries full of sensitive information. First, a desensitization pipeline builds rule sets from security standards, uses an LLM to detect sensitive content, and runs context-aware desensitization that retains business logic while wiping private details. Second, a teacher model generates SQL from desensitized text to build high-quality training samples, which fine-tunes a lightweight student model to inherit domain skills without privacy hazards. Title: Scaffolding the scaffold: Co-evolving human-centered boundaries for genai in education
Source title: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications
Abstract: Current educational approaches often treat GenAI access as binary, permit or prohibit, failing to accommodate learning's developmental nature. This one-size-fits-all approach risks either depriving students of valuable learning opportunities or enabling over-reliance that undermines skill development. While recent work explores instructor-configurable GenAI, no approach treats governance as an adaptive per-student scaffold based on demonstrated competency. We propose co-evolving boundaries: GenAI constraints that evolve dynamically with student competency. Grounded in pedagogical theories (Zone of Proximal Development, scaffolding, mastery learning) and technical capabilities (learning analytics, configurable GenAI), adaptive boundaries would evolve through three developmental stages negotiated among students, teachers, and GenAI systems: restrictive scaffolding for novices, selective access with over-reliance monitoring for intermediates, and open collaboration for advanced students. We present four research questions addressing boundary negotiation, competency detection, transparency, and evaluation. Title: Causal–Semantic Spatiotemporal Traffic Flow Forecasting for Expressway UAV Pre-Deployment Using ETC Gantry Networks
Source title: ISPRS International Journal of Geo-Information
Abstract: Expressway unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) pre-deployment is a geospatial decision-support task that requires reliable road-segment-level traffic flow prediction based on spatial sensing networks. In addition, complex models often fail to meet the computational requirements of edge-device deployment. Based on electronic toll collection (ETC) gantry data, this study proposes a causal–semantic spatiotemporal forecasting framework for long-term traffic flow prediction with a 24 h forecasting horizon. First, conditional Granger causality analysis is used to construct a directed causal prior graph that characterizes traffic propagation relationships among expressway segments. Second, scenario-semantic priors generated by a large language model are introduced to describe atypical traffic conditions. Then, causal structural priors and scenario-semantic priors are integrated into a teacher model and transferred to a lightweight student model through response-level and feature-level knowledge distillation. Experiments using expressway data from Hubei Province, China, show that the proposed model achieves the best overall performance in the typical scenario and competitive performance in the atypical scenario. Abstract: The widespread application of generative AI in higher education has raised questions about how AI usage behaviors relate to students’ development of digital literacy. Title: Predicting English learning performance in vocational colleges using explainable large language models
Source title: Discover Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: English proficiency prediction is an important task in vocational education because it is helpful in support teaching evaluation, personalized learning and early academic intervention. Traditional methods for predicting student performance mainly use structured educational properties such as test scores, classroom participation and attendance records. Although these methods can achieve certain prediction results, they often pay no attention to the semantic relationships contained in the students’ overall learning portfolios and have limited interpretability. To address this problem, this study proposes an interpretable large language model-based framework to predict English proficiency. Firstly, student learning records are transformed into natural language prompts, and semantic embeddings are learned using large language models. At the same time, structured educational features are standardized and encoded to build a structured representation. Then, a gated multimodal fusion module is designed to adaptively fuse semantic information and structured information. Finally, residual attention multi-layer perceptrons are used to classify the fused features to predict the students’ English proficiency. The experiment was carried out on a dataset of 200 student records from a vocational college for English learning. The results showed that the proposed model achieved an accuracy rate of 92.5% and a weighted F1 score of 91.3%, which is better than several traditional machine learning baseline models. Further analysis showed that the gated fusion mechanism could integrate semantic information and structured information. Feature importance analysis and case studies also shown that the proposed framework could provide interpretable prediction results and personalized learning recommendations. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Mapping AI related research in education through bibliometric analysis across four selected journals from 2020 to 2025

Abstract: Artificial intelligence in education (AIED) has expanded rapidly since the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, yet recent development remains insufficiently mapped. This study examines publication growth, thematic change, citation impact, journal profiles and collaboration structure in AI-related research published in four selected journals between 2020 and 2025: Interactive learning environments (ILE), Computers and education: artificial intelligence (CAEAI), Journal of learning analytics (JLA) and International journal of artificial intelligence in education (IJAIED). Keyword clustering placed generative AI in the motor-theme quadrant. Co-authorship analysis identified a fragmented prolific core of 74 authors in the largest connected component, divided into eight sub-groups and linked by authors with high betweenness centrality. Title: Reframing educational management in the digital era: A bibliometric and conceptual analysis

Abstract: This study traced the intellectual development and thematic evolution of educational management research amid digital transformation and global educational change. These insights yield a structured future research agenda spanning eight critical frontiers, including generative AI governance, learning analytics, blockchain credentialing, cybersecurity, digital equity, AI ethics, data-driven decision-making, and organisational resilience. Title: The adoption gap in adaptive learning path generation: an analytical review of barriers and operational requirements
Source title: Frontiers in Computer Science
Abstract: Introduction – Adaptive learning path generation (ALPG) aims to personalize the selection and sequencing of learning activities based on learner state and instructional goals. Despite decades of research and multiple methodological waves, ranging from intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) and metaheuristic optimization to reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM)-based approaches, its adoption in operational learning environments remains limited. Methods – This paper employs an iterative literature review design combining an umbrella review of existing surveys with a supplementary systematic search on adoption, barriers, and operational conditions. The findings are synthesized through qualitative thematic aggregation to identify recurring barriers, derive adoption-critical requirements, and develop a requirement-based analytical framework for assessing ALPG methods. Results – The analysis reveals a persistent research-practice gap. Most ALPG approaches remain at the level of prototypes, course-level implementations, or domain-specific systems, while mainstream platforms rely on rule-based personalization. The literature identifies interdependent barriers across algorithmic, data-related, pedagogical, technical, organizational, human, and ethical dimensions. These barriers can be reframed as operational requirements, including scalability, robust learner modeling, pedagogical grounding, system integration, governance compliance, and human-centered design. Discussion – The findings indicate that ALPG is not only a technical sequencing problem but a sociotechnical orchestration problem. The paper contributes a requirement-based framework that links methodological design choices to adoption-relevant conditions and enables a structured assessment of practical feasibility. Title: Rank-aware agglomeration of foundation models for immunohistochemistry image cell counting

Abstract: Accurate cell counting in immunohistochemistry (IHC) images is critical for quantifying protein expression and aiding cancer diagnosis. However, the task remains challenging due to the chromogen overlap, variable biomarker staining, and diverse cellular morphologies. Regression-based counting methods offer advantages over detection-based ones in handling overlapped cells, yet rarely support end-to-end multi-class counting. Moreover, the potential of foundation models remains largely underexplored in this paradigm. To address these limitations, we propose a rank-aware agglomeration framework that selectively distills knowledge from multiple strong foundation models, leveraging their complementary representations to handle IHC heterogeneity and obtain a compact yet effective student model, CountIHC. Unlike prior task-agnostic agglomeration strategies that either treat all teachers equally or rely on feature similarity, we design a Rank-Aware Teacher Selecting (RATS) strategy that models global-to-local patch rankings to assess each teacher’s inherent counting capacity and enable sample-wise teacher selection. For multi-class cell counting, we introduce a fine-tuning stage that reformulates the task as vision–language alignment. Discrete semantic anchors derived from structured text prompts encode both category and quantity information, guiding the regression of class-specific density maps and improving counting for overlapping cells. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CountIHC surpasses state-of-the-art methods across 12 IHC biomarkers and 5 tissue types, while exhibiting high agreement with pathologists’ assessments. Abstract: To address the limitations of large language models (LLMs) in source code vulnerability detection—namely insufficient utilization of program structural information, unstable reasoning processes, and high fine-tuning costs—we propose a vulnerability detection framework that integrates graph-based representations with LLM reasoning capabilities. Title: A Closed-Loop Artificial Intelligence System for Process-Oriented Student Assessment and Early Performance Prediction in Higher Education
Source title: Applied Sciences (Switzerland)
Abstract: The increasing amount of detailed learning data in higher education has shifted assessment methods from traditional scores to continuous assessment of student learning performance. This paper presents an applied closed-loop AI system that supports early performance prediction, informed risk decision-making, and personalized intervention planning. The system utilizes aggregated weekly data from learning management systems, including self-regulated learning metrics and participation indicators. A supervised regression model predicts near-future learning performance while employing chronological training strategies to prevent information leakage. Emphasizing decision-driven assessment, the system translates predictive outputs into a resource-sensitive decision framework to identify students requiring early support. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques enhance the model’s transparency, providing insights into key learning factors and individual student-level explanations. The system generates actionable recommendations based on these insights. Its closed-loop architecture integrates data collection, prediction, interpretation, recommendation generation, and feedback logging, allowing instructors to monitor learning pathways and examine subsequent learning outcomes. Title: ORCHID-RANKER: An Agentic Adaptive Recommender for Education with Privacy Guarantees
Source title: Proceedings of the ACM Symposium on Applied Computing
Abstract: Digital learning platforms often recommend what activity a student should do next. They usually base this on a few simple signals, such as whether the student accepted the activity, answered correctly, and how long it took. These systems are often complex and hard for teachers to understand or control, and they also need to protect student privacy. We present ORCHID-RANKER, a simple decision module that can be added to existing recommenders in such platforms without changing them. It keeps track of three things for each learner: how ready they seem (knowledge), how willing they seem (engagement), and how uncertain the system is. Using this information, it adjusts a few simple "dials": how difficult the next activities should be, how much to explore new content, how varied the list of activities is, and how many activities to show. The goal is to keep learners in a "just right"zone where tasks are not too easy and not too hard, and to keep them engaged. Behind this decision module, the underlying models are trained with strong privacy protection (differential privacy), so that individual students cannot be easily identified from the data. In simulations on two real course datasets (OULAD and EdNet), ORCHID-RANKER led to higher learning and engagement than standard recommendation methods, while still maintaining formal privacy guarantees.  © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: A Study on the Innovative Model of Integrating AI into Fundamental Foreign Language Education
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Generative Artificial Intelligence and Education, GAIE 2026
Abstract: This study proposes and implements an innovative artificial intelligence (AI) system tailored for foundational foreign language education, aiming to provide a practical, scalable, and technology-driven solution for traditional language instruction. The engine adopts a modular architecture that deeply integrates state-of-the-art natural language processing (NLP) techniques with adaptive learning algorithms. Its core technical stack comprises three key components: (1) a speech recognition and pronunciation assessment module based on the Wav2Vec 2.0 pre-trained model combined with a Transformer architecture; (2) a personalized learning path recommendation engine that fuses Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) with collaborative filtering algorithms; and (3) a real-time feedback and interaction module that combines a rule-based engine with a fine-tuned large language model (LLM). The entire system is deployed on a local educational cloud platform and seamlessly integrates with mainstream Learning Management Systems (LMS) via RESTful APIs. To evaluate the technical efficacy and pedagogical value of the AI engine, the study conducted an 8-week controlled A/B test involving 32 students. Quantitative analysis revealed that, compared to the baseline system, the optimized AI engine demonstrated superior performance across multiple key technical metrics: the average system response time was reduced to 760 milliseconds, and the average CPU utilization rate was only 32.4%. Moreover, its intelligent features significantly enhanced instructional outcomes, as evidenced by a 27.3% increase in exercise completion rate, a 26.4% rise in the adoption rate of error-correction suggestions, and a high alignment (Jaccard coefficient of 0.81) between the system-generated content and the knowledge points assessed by instructors. Learning outcome assessments further confirmed that students in the experimental group showed significant improvement across all four language skills—listening, speaking, reading, and writing—with the most notable gain observed in speaking proficiency (+15.7%). This study not only empirically demonstrates the positive value of AI in foreign language education but, more importantly, constructs and validates a lightweight, modular, and reusable AI-powered instructional technology stack. This achievement provides a robust technical paradigm and practical reference for resource-constrained educational settings—such as primary and secondary schools—and significantly advances the deep integration of information technology and language education from conceptual vision toward large-scale implementation. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Generalised Distillation of Geospatial Foundation Models
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) are large-scale models with millions of parameters, pre-trained on vast amounts of data to support diverse downstream tasks. However, they are typically computationally demanding, which restricts deployment in resource-limited environments. Furthermore, they are predominantly trained using optical data despite the inherent limitations of this modality due to natural phenomena such as cloud cover and atmospheric conditions. Our work aims to leverage multiple modalities by specifically transferring knowledge from a multimodal teacher using optical and radar data, to train a radar-only student model. To ensure computational efficiency, we apply offline feature-based knowledge distillation to a frozen TerraMind-B teacher to compress its multimodal knowledge into a lightweight unimodal TerraMind-S student model. Despite using a smaller student architecture, our distillation approach outperforms TerraMind’s state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance on radar data. Lastly, we find that the later layers are more important in enhancing the performance of the student model and that distillation performance is thematically dependent. Title: Using LLMs for Knowledge Component-Level Correctness Labeling in Open-Ended Coding Problems

Abstract: Fine-grained skill representations, commonly referred to as knowledge components (KCs), are fundamental to many approaches in student modeling and learning analytics. Simply propagating problem-level correctness to all associated KCs obscures partial mastery and often leads to poorly fitted learning curves. Title: A Rubric-Grounded LLM Feedback Framework for Academic Writing: An Empirical Study in an Information-Enhanced Classroom Setting
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Big Data and Informatization Education, ICBDIE 2026
Abstract: Artificial intelligence-based writing feedback has been increasingly adopted in higher education to address constraints related to instructional time and feedback scalability; however, its effectiveness is often undermined by weak alignment with course evaluation standards. To address this limitation, this study empirically examines whether embedding assessment rubrics as explicit constraints in artificial intelligence-generated feedback can improve academic writing outcomes in an informatization education context. A rubric-constrained feedback framework was implemented in an undergraduate academic writing course using a quasi-experimental design (N=66), in which students were assigned to either an experimental group receiving rubric-constrained feedback or a control group receiving unconstrained feedback. Writing performance was measured through score improvements between initial and final drafts, while feedback quality was independently evaluated by instructors. The results show that the experimental group achieved significantly greater overall writing improvement than the control group (t(64)=4.36, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.98), with dimension-level analyses revealing stronger gains in argumentation, text organization, and evidence use. In addition, instructor ratings indicate that rubric-constrained feedback outperforms unconstrained feedback in alignment with evaluation standards, specificity, and practical usability (all p<0.01), demonstrating large effect sizes in key dimensions. These findings suggest that assessment rubrics serve as an effective mediating mechanism between instructional objectives and artificial intelligence-generated feedback, and that embedding artificial intelligence tools within established evaluation frameworks can substantially enhance both learning outcomes and feedback quality, offering practical guidance for data-driven instructional design in informatization education. © 2026 Copyright held by the owner/author(s).

Title: Using Artificial Intelligence in Mobile Learning for Students of Technical Specialties

Title: The Limits of Text-Only LLMs for Think-Aloud Transcript Correction: A Multimodal Comparison in the Context of a Puzzle Video Game
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Think-aloud protocols provide valuable insights into learners’ reasoning, but transcribing verbal data is time-consuming. Automatic speech recognition (ASR) can reduce this burden but can also introduce errors. By analyzing 1,900 utterances from six English think-aloud transcripts of university students playing a puzzle game, we compared text-only and multimodal audio/video approaches to explore whether large language models (LLMs) can correct these errors. Three researchers created reference transcripts by reviewing original audio and video recordings. We compared four prompting strategies with Claude Sonnet 4.5 (text-only) and Gemini 2.5 Flash (multimodal). This identified text-detectable errors (13.6% of utterances), correctable using domain context (game rules and terminology), and Audio/Video-Dependent errors (7.6%) requiring the original recording. For text-detectable errors, all text-only strategies achieved high precision (86–90%) and specificity (>97%). Few-shot with extended thinking achieved the highest recall (89.1%), significantly outperforming zero-shot (84.0%, p=.026). The text-only approach matched the multimodal model on text-detectable errors (89.1% vs. 86.8%, p=.440). A direct re-transcription condition (audio/video only, no source text) achieved substantially lower accuracy (82.8%) and missed 8.5% of utterances, demonstrating that correction-based workflows outperform re-transcription. However, the multimodal approach was essential for Audio/Video-Dependent errors (55.2% vs. ∼2% recall, p<.001). These findings suggest that text-only LLMs can effectively reduce transcript-correction effort, whereas multimodal approaches are necessary when higher accuracy is required. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Unified Explainable Predictive Analytics Pipeline for Learning Management Systems
Source title: SN Computer Science
Abstract: High student attrition and inconsistent academic performance remain persistent challenges in higher education, motivating the development of reliable and interpretable predictive decision-support systems. Learning Management Systems (LMS) generate rich behavioural and assessment data; however, existing predictive learning analytics studies often exhibit limited generalizability and insufficient explainability. This study proposes a unified predictive analytics pipeline for LMS data that integrates systematic preprocessing, feature engineering and selection, multi-model benchmarking, handling of class imbalance, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI). The study benchmarks classical Machine Learning (ML), Ensemble, and Deep Learning (DL) models on two heterogeneous LMS datasets: OULAD for binary dropout prediction and Offee for multi-class grade prediction. The proposed pipeline operationalises a complete predict–explain–act educational workflow that combines imbalance-aware prediction with intervention-oriented explainability within a unified decision-support architecture. Title: Edge AI-Enabled PMU Event Classification With Knowledge Distillation and Federated Learning
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Smart Grid
Abstract: Phasor Measurement Units (PMUs) enable analysis and classification of events and abnormalities in modern power systems. However, in large and geographically dispersed networks, centralizing PMU data streams for sub-second decisions is hindered by cross-regional data-sharing restrictions, multi-layer aggregation, as well as communication delays and jitter. Purely local training at the network edge on the PMU devices themselves can avoid these bottlenecks but lacks exposure to diverse operating conditions, leading to suboptimal models. This tension calls for methods that retain data locality and privacy while sharing knowledge efficiently. To this end, this paper proposes an edge AI framework that integrates knowledge distillation and federated learning, driven by the core requirement of different data-sharing constraints. First, we assume a trusted data center, where we develop a large language model-based teacher model that is fine-tuned on global data and efficiently transfers knowledge into student models trained locally via knowledge distillation. Next, we relax such an assumption and design a fair federated learning framework that exchanges gradient information among edge models while enforcing Pareto-optimal fairness to ensure stable and balanced performance. We also customize a lightweight neural network tailored for on-device deployment. With fewer than 5,000 parameters, the model adopts a compact end-to-end architecture to effectively characterize temporal dynamics and frequency-domain information in PMU time series, thereby achieving both high efficiency and strong representational capability. Experiments conducted on real-world PMU measurements demonstrate the superior performance of our framework, and ablation studies further confirm the unique contributions of each design component. © 2010 IEEE.

Title: From Predictive Models to Actionable Recommendations: A Survey of Counterfactual Approaches in Student Dropout
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Student dropout remains a critical challenge in global education, representing a significant loss of human capital. Although data-driven approaches like predictive modeling have achieved high accuracy in identifying at-risk students, a “trust gap” persists among educators. Prediction alone is insufficient; stakeholders require interpretable insights to guide effective intervention. This survey explores the paradigm shift from passive “black-box” detection to “actionable prescription” through the lens of Counterfactual Explanations (CFE). We analyze 23 primary studies published between 2021 and 2026, categorizing them using a novel Intervention Pipeline taxonomy that bridges four levels: Identification (predictive models), Interpretation (XAI), Visual Analytics (interactive visualization and human-in-the-loop analysis), and Actionable Recommendations (counterfactuals). Adopting an analytical framework, we systematically interrogate the literature regarding variable risk definitions, data source diversity, prediction horizons, and feature actionability. Our analysis reveals a critical disconnect: while many models prioritize accuracy using immutable features, few focus on the actionable variables necessary for generating feasible pedagogical recommendations. We conclude that while CFE offers a promising path for personalized support, future research must address challenges regarding causal validity, explanation stability, and scalability (individual vs. institutional) to successfully bridge the gap between algorithmic output and practical pedagogical action. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Research on the integration of social practice resources in higher education institutions based on deep learning and data mining algorithms
Source title: Discover Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: The integration of social practice resources in higher education provides experiential, emphatic, and collaborative learning. Conventional techniques are limited by their inability to involve situational connections and nonlinear interactions between multifaceted datasets, resulting in lower precision. To address these challenges, an intelligent deep learning (DL)-driven framework is developed for efficient integration and optimization of social practice resources with data mining technology. Title: Mapping of Artificial Intelligence Applications and their Impacts on Academic Performance in Higher Education (2020–2025): A Systematic and Bibliometric Literature Review

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used in higher education, yet evidence concerning its relationship with academic performance remains fragmented across adoption studies, predictive models and evaluations of learning outcomes. Title: Adaptive Multi-Agent Learning Systems: A Reinforcement Learning Framework with LLM-Powered Assessment for Personalized Online Education and study
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Big Data and Informatization Education, ICBDIE 2026
Abstract: Online education platforms face persistent challenges in delivering effective personalized learning at scale. Title: Interpretable knowledge tracing via explicit–implicit alignment
Source title: Knowledge-Based Systems
Abstract: Interpretability in Knowledge Tracing (KT) is crucial for personalized learning. Current mainstream Deep Learning-based KT (DLKT) achieves strong predictive performance with ID-based representations, but students’ latent knowledge states remain opaque to teachers and learners. Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate human-readable text, but explanations from existing LLM-augmented KT approaches are either detached from the predictive state or insensitive to individual trajectories. To bridge this gap, we propose Interpretable Knowledge Tracing via Explicit–Implicit Alignment (IKT-EIA), which anchors implicit student knowledge representations with LLM-derived explicit textual insights. IKT-EIA consists of: (1) Context-Guided Knowledge Integration (CGKI) uses LLMs to generate trajectory-aware textual knowledge from student metadata; (2) Query-Driven Knowledge State Alignment (QKSA) treats the implicit state as a query to retrieve and fuse explicit semantics, producing an aligned knowledge state that supports subsequent explanation analysis; (3) Personalized Explainability Adaptation (PEA) generates structured and adaptive feedback by reading the aligned state together with raw interaction records, tailoring explanations to students’ evolving mastery. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that IKT-EIA maintains competitive predictive performance while producing state-aware explanations that were found useful in a controlled evaluation setting. © 2026

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped higher education over six decades, evolving from drill-and-practice programs to adaptive cognitive tutors and, most recently, transformer-based generative models. Abstract: The pervasive integration of artificial intelligence across e-commerce ecosystems has fundamentally transformed the competitive landscape, rendering systematic and reproducible platform evaluation frameworks an operational necessity rather than an academic exercise. Inter-agent consensus was synthesized through geometric mean aggregation, with consistency verification conducted via BWM’s xi* indicator and inter-round stability assessed through coefficient of variation analysis. Results reveal that Transaction Security and Trust achieves the highest dimension-level weight (w = 0.248), followed by AI Recommendation Effectiveness (w = 0.213), with Personal Data Protection (G = 0.0750), Recommendation Accuracy (G = 0.0607), and Transaction Transparency (G = 0.0549) emerging as the three highest globally ranked sub-criteria. Sensitivity analysis under perturbations of ±10% and ±20% demonstrates that the top-five priority indicators are structurally stable. Title: HKD-CPI: high-order knowledge distillation enhanced inductive compound-protein interaction prediction
Source title: Bioinformatics
Abstract: Motivation: Accurately identifying compound–protein interactions (CPIs) is critical for accelerating drug discovery. Recent deep learning methods have achieved impressive results, yet they primarily focus on local structures and neighborhood information, often overlooking high-order interaction patterns shared among similar molecules. Results: In this paper, we propose HKD-CPI, a high-order knowledge-enhanced inductive framework designed to improve generalization to unseen compound–protein pairs. Specifically, HKD-CPI introduces a molecular graph tokenization mechanism that aligns compound molecular graph features with token embeddings from sequence-pretrained large language models (LLMs), effectively infusing sequence-derived semantics into structural representations. To capture shared interaction patterns among functionally similar biomolecules, we construct a hypergraph-based representation to model high-order relationships between feature-similar compound/protein groups and their binding partners. Furthermore, a knowledge distillation strategy is further adopted to transfer high-order interaction knowledge from the hypergraph to a lightweight student model, enabling efficient and robust CPI prediction. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HKD-CPI outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in inductive CPI prediction tasks. In particular, it achieves an average improvement of 4.94% in AUROC and 3.64% in AUPRC over the best-performing baseline across five benchmark datasets. Title: Enhancing 100 m wind speed forecasts in China based on CatBoost feature selection and stacking ensemble learning

Abstract: Wind turbine hub-height wind speed forecast is a key factor affecting the stable operation of power grids, but its high uncertainty and chaotic fluctuations make accurate wind speed forecast challenging. This perspective argues that the field’s next inflection point lies not in richer sensors alone but in the interpretive layer that turns signals into states. Title: First-Order Cross-Domain Meta Learning for Few-Shot Remote Sensing Object Classification
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
Abstract: Remote sensing images exhibit intrinsic domain complexity arising from multi-source sensor variances, which heterogeneity fundamentally challenges conventional cross-domain few-shot methods that assume simple distribution shifts. Addressing this, we propose a first-order Cross-Domain Meta Learning (CDML) for few-shot remote sensing object classification. CDML implements a dual-stage domain adaptation task as the fundamental meta-learning unit, and includes a cross-domain meta-train phase (CDMTrain) and a cross-domain meta-test phase (CDMTest). In CDMTrain, we propose an inner-loop multi-domain few-shot task sampling, which enables a teacher model encapsulate both cross-category discriminative features and authentic inter-domain distributional divergence. This alternating cyclic learning paradigm captures genuine domain shifts, with each update direction progressively guiding the model toward parameters that balance multi-domain performance. In CDMTest, we evaluate a domain diversity enhancement by transferring teacher parameters to the student model for cross-domain capability assessment on the reserved pseudo-unseen domain. The task-level design progressively improves domain generalization through iterative domain adaptive task learning. Meanwhile, to mitigate the conflicts and inadequacies caused by multi-domain scenarios, we propose a learnable affine transformation model. It adaptively learns affine transformation parameters through intermediate layer features to fine-tune the update direction. Extensive experiments on five remote sensing classification benchmarks demonstrate a superior performance of the proposed method compared with the state-of-the-art methods. © 1979-2012 IEEE.
