Title: A Comprehensive Evaluation of Generative Models for Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Student Data
Source title: IEEE Access
Abstract: Privacy regulations and institutional policies limit the sharing of educational data, constraining reproducibility in learning analytics. Prior evaluations of synthetic data on benchmarks such as OULAD have examined statistical or adversarial synthesizers in isolation, rarely jointly assessing fidelity, utility, privacy, and explainability. We compare three synthesis paradigms, statistical (Gaussian Copula), adversarial (CTGAN), and diffusion-based (TabDDPM), on two benchmarks (OULAD: 32,593 records; ASSISTments: 8,519) across five evaluation axes: distributional fidelity (SDMetrics), downstream utility (Train on Synthetic, Test on Real), discriminative realism (classifier two-sample test), membership-inference privacy, and feature-importance preservation (SHAP). The pipeline is repeated over five random seeds with bootstrap confidence intervals and Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests (α ′ approx ~0.0028 ). Four findings emerge: First, TabDDPM delivers the strongest classification utility: on OULAD, a Random Forest achieves TSTR AUC = 0.962~pm ~0.001 , within 0.5 percentage points of the real-data baseline. Second, all synthesizers exhibit near-chance membership-inference risk under the evaluated kNN-based threat model (worst-case effective AUC ≤ 0.527 ). Third, distributional fidelity does not predict task utility; CTGAN scores highest on SDMetrics yet does not yield the smallest utility gap. Fourth, TabDDPM best preserves real-data feature-importance rankings on OULAD (Spearman ρ =0.846 , p < 0.001). ASSISTments SHAP correlations (ρ ~ ge 0.950 ) reflect a low-dimensionality ceiling effect rather than meaningful synthesis quality differences. These results provide task-driven guidance for selecting a synthesizer in learning analytics. Scope is limited to static tabular benchmarks; temporal, sequential, multimodal, and fairness-aware synthesis remain outside the present scope. Runtime results are based on CPU execution, so neural synthesizers may run faster under GPU acceleration.  © 2013 IEEE.

Title: A Hybrid Ensemble Learning Approach Using Random Forest and Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting Predicting Student Academic Performance
Source title: Proceedings of 3rd International Conference on Machine Learning and Autonomous Systems, ICMLAS 2026
Abstract: Predicting student success is an important task in educational data mining that has applications in a range of areas including early intervention and personalized learning. This study proposed a hybrid ensemble learning model that exploits the combined strengths of Random Forest (RF) and Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting (HGB) using a stacking approach with Logistic Regression as a meta-learner. The UCI / Kaggle Student Performance dataset was used to support training and test the model, containing demographic, social, and academic data regarding 395 secondary school students. The final grade (G3) was used to predict a binary pass/fail outcome. The hybrid model demonstrated a better performance than all the individual classifiers with an overall test set accuracy of 87.34%, precision of 95.74%, recall of 84.91%, and F1-score of 90.00%. This performance outpaces several recent studies, which included a 2024 SAIE study that reports only 77.42% accuracy in predicting student grades with a standalone Random Forest model. The feature importance analysis indicated that prior grades G1 and G2, parental education, and study time were of high importance. Our hybrid model has high accuracy and is interpretable, providing a means for educators and policymakers to identify students at risk academically and execute timely interventions. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Charting the Future of Education: Technology, Ethics, and Equity

Abstract: This concluding chapter brings the volume full circle, synthesising insights across four themes to show how Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) is reshaping higher education and to chart pathways grounded in ethics, equity, and sustainability. TEL has moved from a supportive add-on to a structural imperative, reshaping curriculum, assessment, student support, and institutional culture. Central is an educator agency: teachers’ design knowledge (e.g., TPACK) and identity work mediate whether tools translate into learning. Across the themes, contributors demonstrate how AI, immersive media, and learning analytics can widen opportunity while raising equity, integrity, and access challenges. We advance a human-in-the-loop approach to assessment—aligning AI feedback with explicit outcomes, transparency for students, and moderated professional judgement—and a rights-based governance stance: privacy by design, data minimisation, explainability, and proportionate monitoring. Global cases from Asia, Europe, and Australasia underline that shared tools are enacted locally: CALL differentiation, HyFlex delivery, and virtual-production studios succeed only when embedded in institutional ecosystems of policy, workload, learning design, and AV/IT support. Looking ahead, generative AI, immersive production, and micro-credentialing will matter—but design, governance, and capability will matter more. We close with role-specific commitments and a near-term action agenda to make TEL inclusive, ethical, and sustainable. © 2026 selection and editorial matter, Ida Fatimawati Adi Badiozaman and Augustus Raymond Segar.

Title: Learning Analytics by Design: Safeguarding Metadata for AI Services Augmenting Open-Source Middleware with LRS Functionality
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Modern learning platforms are modular ecosystems with decentralized storage of content, offerings, and metadata. LLM-based chatbots are increasingly integrated to support learners in their educational journey. This development highlights the importance of collecting and analyzing learning data to enable personalized and adaptive e-learning applications that improve outcomes across different offerings. Based on operational research [1] with the German Armed Forces (Bundeswehr, Bw), we identified the need for decentralized, middleware-based Learning Record Store (LRS) solutions that respect organizational policies for data governance, privacy, federated identities, and interoperability, using the Experience API (xAPI) as the standard for tracking learning experiences. Current literature reveals a significant gap in the LRS landscape. Existing approaches often lack mechanisms for effective data flow control, interoperability, and strict data separation in decentralized environments. They also fail to maintain optimized metadata for AI services. To address these shortcomings, this research examines the organizational and technical requirements for a decentralized, middleware-based LRS. Our contribution is a novel concept designed to function as a network of data enclaves, enabling seamless queries and semantic control across the organization. Title: Next-Gen Engagement Metric: A Novel Index for Tracking Student Participation in Online Synchronous Learning
Source title: IEEE Global Engineering Education Conference, EDUCON
Abstract: The rapid expansion of synchronous online learning in higher education has intensified the need for reliable and interpretable approaches to monitoring student engagement during live virtual classes. While platforms such as Zoom and Microsoft Teams enable real-time interaction, they significantly reduce educators' access to traditional engagement cues, including body language, facial expressions, and spontaneous interaction. Existing engagement frameworks are largely designed for face-to-face or asynchronous contexts and often rely on retrospective indicators, limiting their effectiveness for timely pedagogical intervention. This paper proposes the Next-Generation Engagement Metric (NGEM), operationalized through an Enhanced Engagement Index (eEI), as a theory-informed composite measure of student engagement in synchronous online learning environments. The eEI integrates behavioural, cognitive, affective-proxy, and contextual indicators grounded in established multidimensional engagement theory. Emotional engagement is not detected directly through emotion-recognition technologies; instead, it is inferred via observable behavioural patterns such as responsiveness, voluntary participation, and engagement consistency, supporting ethical and non-intrusive deployment. The eEI is formulated as a hierarchical weighted index, with indicator weights derived from structured higher-education educator focus groups to reflect pedagogical priorities. To enable controlled experimentation under privacy and data-access constraints, the study employs a hybrid dataset combining distributions informed by the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD) with rule-based synthetic indicators representing synchronous learning behaviours. Supervised machine learning models (Decision Tree and Random Forest) are used to examine alignment between eEI-based engagement tiers and predictive patterns, with evaluation including cross-validation, class-wise metrics, and confusion matrix analysis. Results indicate consistent alignment between the eEI and predictive outputs, with active participation indicators contributing more strongly than passive signals. Findings are interpreted cautiously, acknowledging limitations related to synthetic data realism, platform dependency, and generalisability. NGEM is positioned as an educator-centred decision-support metric rather than an automated evaluative system, with future work focusing on validation using authentic synchronous learning datasets and educator-led evaluation. The findings demonstrate how human-centred, AI-enabled engagement analytics can support ethical, timely intervention and sustainable innovation in digitally transformed higher education. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Knowledge Tracing Models in Educational Data Mining: Historical Evolution, Categorization, and Empirical Evaluation
Source title: IEEE Access
Abstract: This article analyses computational models of Knowledge Tracing (KT), which address the complex sequence-modelling task of predicting dynamic, unobservable latent user states from historical interaction logs. First, we propose a comprehensive taxonomy identifying nine distinct and interconnected KT model families: psychometric; Bayesian; machine learning; deep learning; graph-based; temporal/sequential; multi-task; contrastive/self-supervised; and domain-adaptive. Secondly, we trace the historical evolution of KT architectures, from the foundational psychometric methods of the 1950s to the modern integration of attention mechanisms and graph neural networks. Thirdly, we systematically evaluate nine lightweight representative computational models - one from each category - across two large-scale datasets: ASSISTments 09-10 and DigiArvi 2025. We measure predictive calibration using accuracy, F1 score, ROC-AUC, average precision, and log loss under a strict computational time budget. Finally, our rigorous empirical analysis demonstrates that multi-task and temporal/sequential architectures yield the highest performance. Specifically, Fine-Grained Knowledge Tracing (FKT) achieved the best results on the DigiArvi dataset (accuracy: 0.77; F1 score: 0.85), while Temporal Item Response Theory (TIRT) performed best on the ASSISTments dataset (accuracy: 0.70; F1 score: 0.75). Traditional baselines, such as Logistic Regression (LR), remain highly competitive. Consequently, we advocate a shift towards 'Green AI' and standardized benchmarking to address the field's fragmented evaluation standards, as we identify diminishing returns from increasing model complexity. Future research must leverage generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and causal inference to move beyond simple prediction toward agentic AI systems capable of active pedagogical intervention.  © 2013 IEEE.

Title: From Gaze to Insight: Bridging Human Visual Attention and Vision Language Model Explanation for Weakly-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging
Abstract: Medical image segmentation remains challenging due to the high cost of pixel-level annotations for training. In the context of weak supervision, clinician gaze data captures regions of diagnostic interest; however, its sparsity limits its use for segmentation. In contrast, vision-language models (VLMs) provide semantic context through textual descriptions but lack the explanation precision required. Recognizing that neither source alone suffices, we propose a teacher-student framework that integrates both gaze and language supervision, leveraging their complementary strengths. Our key insight is that gaze data indicates 'where' clinicians focus during diagnosis, while VLMs explain 'why' those regions are significant. To implement this, the teacher model first learns from gaze points enhanced by VLM-generated descriptions of lesion morphology, establishing a foundation for guiding the student model. The teacher then directs the student through three strategies: 1) Multi-scale feature alignment to fuse visual cues with textual semantics; 2) Confidence-weighted consistency constraints to focus on reliable predictions; 3) Adaptive masking to limit error propagation in uncertain areas. Experiments on the Kvasir-SEG, NCI-ISBI, and ISIC datasets show that our method achieves Dice scores of 80.78%, 80.53%, and 84.22%, respectively - improving 3-5% over gaze baselines without increasing the annotation burden. By preserving correlations among predictions, gaze data, and lesion descriptions, our framework also maintains clinical interpretability. This work illustrates how integrating human visual attention with AI-generated semantic context can effectively overcome the limitations of individual weak supervision signals, thereby advancing the development of deployable, annotation-efficient medical AI systems. Title: Leveraging Generative AI for Cognitive Skill Enhancement in Low-Performing Programming Learners

Abstract: This study investigates the efficacy of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in enhancing cognitive programming skills specifically problem decomposition, algorithmic thinking, and debuggingamong low-performing novice learners. We developed and deployed a structured pedagogical intervention, the Generative AI-Driven Cognitive Scaffolding (GAIDCS) framework, which integrates a Large Language Model (LLM) tutor into a 12-week introductory Python course. The framework employs prompt engineering to guide the AI in providing Socratic questioning, incremental code generation, and misconceptiontargeted feedback, rather than direct solutions. Participants (N=1 2 0) were divided into an experimental group (n=60) using the GAIDCS framework and a control group (n=60) using traditional teaching aids. Cognitive skill proficiency was measured via a validated pre-test and post-test instrument. Additionally, learning traces (prompt history, code versions) were analyzed for metacognitive engagement. Furthermore, analysis of learning traces indicated a 65 % increase in metacognitive prompts ('explain your approach') issued by learners in the later weeks, correlating with higher post-test gains (r=0.71). These findings suggest that strategically scaffolded GenAI interactions can significantly enhance core cognitive programming skills by promoting active reasoning and mitigating overreliance. The study posits that the key to efficacy lies not in the AI's capability to generate code, but in its structured role as a reflective partner that externalizes and guides the problem-solving process for struggling learners. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: AI-Augmented Career Advising in Universities: Digital Ethics and Security concerns
Source title: 2026 International Conference on Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics, and AI Applications, ICCSDFAI 2026
Abstract: University career services must deliver scalable, personalized, and equitable support to large student populations while operating with limited advising capacity. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can expand routine guidance, document feedback, and analytics, but its use in career advising raises concerns regarding overreliance, transparency, authorship, fairness, privacy, and security. The aim of this paper is to design, and partially validate through an illustrative deployment scenario, a human-centered, integrity-aware, and institutionally governable service model for AI-augmented career advising, instantiated as MyDU CareerHub, a subsystem of the MyDU Digital University platform. We conduct a PRISMA-aligned review (2018-2026), ground the design in established career-development theory, and propose a five-layer hybrid socio-technical architecture: an integrity gate, a bounded student-facing AI career coach, a role-aware evidence-alignment module, an adviser co-pilot, and institutional analytics, governed by a cross-cutting governance plane. The novelty is threefold: (i) an integrity gate that treats AI-writing signals as formative, appealable indicators rather than punitive evidence; (ii) explicit, enforceable AI-human division-of-labour rules with a security and privacy specification for advising data and interaction logs; and (iii) a reference prototype with an operational metrics suite and a mixed-methods, longitudinal evaluation design. An illustrative case-based validation indicates measurable reductions in routine adviser load and high human review coverage of integrity flags while preserving student authorship. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Evaluating explainable AI attribution methods in neural machine translation via attention-guided knowledge distillation
Source title: Natural Language Processing
Abstract: The study of the attribution of input features to the output of neural network models is an active area of research. While numerous Explainable AI (XAI) techniques have been proposed to interpret these models, the systematic and automated evaluation of these methods in sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models is less explored. This paper introduces a new approach for evaluating explainability methods in transformerbased seq2seq models, building upon the forward simulation of XAI methods. We use teacher-derived attribution maps as a structured side signal to guide a student model, and quantify the utility of different attribution methods through the student’s ability to simulate targets. Using the Inseq library, we extract attribution scores over source–target sequence pairs and inject these scores into the attention mechanism of a student transformer model under four composition operators (addition, multiplication, averaging, and replacement). Across three language pairs (de–en, fr–en, ar–en) and attributions from Marian-MT and mBART models, Attention, Value Zeroing, and Layer Gradient × Activation consistently yield the largest gains in BLEU (and corresponding improvements in chrF) relative to baselines. In contrast, other gradient-based methods (Saliency, Integrated Gradients, DeepLIFT, Input × Gradient, GradientShap) lead to smaller and less consistent improvements. These results suggest that different attribution methods capture distinct signals and that attention-derived attributions better capture the alignment between source and target representations in seq2seq models. Finally, we introduce an Attributor transformer that, given a source–target pair, learns to reconstruct the teacher’s attribution map. Our findings demonstrate that the more accurately the Attributor can reproduce attribution maps, the more useful an injection of those maps is for the downstream task. Title: What should teachers upload to GenAI? A privacy-aware framework for language education
Source title: Asian Journal of Applied Linguistics
Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly intertwined with language education, teachers are expected to integrate AI-supported materials development into their pedagogical practice. However, discussions of GenAI in the field have largely focused on pedagogical innovation and student use, while giving comparatively little attention to the protection of student data and the responsible handling of educational resources. This article argues that data privacy and security should be regarded as core components of teacher GenAI literacy. Adopting a conceptual and practice-oriented approach, it proposes a privacy-aware decision framework for GenAI use that helps teachers align the level of data sensitivity with appropriate GenAI environments, including public cloud-based platforms, institutionally supported services, and offline local GenAI tools. Drawing on research from computer science, cybersecurity, and platform governance, the article suggests practical strategies for reducing privacy risks, including removal, masking, and splitting, before discussing how key considerations relating to student data protection, network security, institutional confidentiality and copyright restrictions may influence teachers' decisions when selecting GenAI tools. Using examples from language materials development, the article illustrates how educators can use GenAI to adapt disciplinary texts, create differentiated learning materials, and generate pedagogical resources while reducing unnecessary disclosure of sensitive information. The article concludes by advocating a more balanced approach to GenAI integration in language education, one that combines pedagogical innovation with informed and responsible data practices. © 2026, University of Hong Kong - Centre for Applied English Studies. Title: Code Quality and Difficulty Aware Programming Knowledge Tracing
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Existing programming knowledge tracking studies have improved model performance by introducing code representation techniques and modeling the relationships between exercises and skills. But the impact of two critical factors, code quality and difficulty, has not been sufficiently explored. This limitation restricts the performance of models in distinguishing learners’ programming ability and accurately modeling their knowledge states. Thus, this paper proposes a Code Quality and Difficulty Aware Programming Knowledge Tracing (CQD-PKT) framework based on attention mechanisms, which aims to explore the impact of three key features of code quality, exercise difficulty and skill difficulty on modeling learners’ programming ability. Specifically, the framework first incorporates difficulty features using a self-attention mechanism to enhance the representation of both exercises and skills. Second, to avoid the subjectivity of manual scoring, the deep pretrained model DeepSeek is employed to achieve automated and objective code quality score. Finally, the framework employs a cross-attention mechanism to evaluate the impact of code quality on programming ability and to capture learners’ application of programming skills with varying difficulty during the coding process. The experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that CQD-PKT outperforms the best baseline model in predicting learners’ future performance. The AUC and ACC are respectively improved by approximately 2% and 1%. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Title: AI-Based Digital Twin System for Personalized Student Learning and Performance Optimization
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference on Circuit, Power and Computing Technologies, ICCPCT 2026
Abstract: The increasing need to have customized and dynamic learning systems has revealed the shortcomings of the traditional fixed learning systems. In this paper, the author introduced an AI-Based Digital Twin System (DTS) that can be used to analyze student learning in real-time and optimize their performance. The suggested system builds a dynamic and constantly changing virtual image of every learner through the combination of academic results, studying behavior, interaction patterns, and learning process. The system uses a machine learning model that uses the Random Forest in subject-wise performance prediction and is supplemented with the Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) methods to give clear and understandable results. The digital twin can dynamically update itself as new data is produced in real time through a mechanism that provides a feedback control mechanism. A What-If Simulation Engine is proposed to facilitate the intelligent decision-making process by enabling the user to conduct a counterfactual analysis to investigate what could have happened in various learning conditions. Moreover, a customized learning pathway generator is an adaptive and structured study recommendation generator based on the needs of individuals. One of the modules is a knowledge graph that represents the relationship between subjects, skills, and career paths, which allows career-oriented and context-specific guidance. The system is deployed as an interactive python based software application and tested on a synthetic dataset of 200 students. The experimental findings show that there are better prediction reliability, personalization and effective decision support when compared to the traditional static systems. The suggested solution justifies the feasibility of the digital twin technology, explainable AI, and adaptive learning strategies integration in contemporary learning settings. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: From Consumers to Creators: Why Educators Must Shape the GenAI Future
Source title: Handbook of Generative AI in Education: Integrating Research into Practice
Abstract: This chapter explores the shift from passive adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools toward educator-led design of AI-powered solutions. While recent advances have made it easier than ever to create custom instructional tools using natural language interfaces, many technologies remain disconnected from classroom realities. Past experiences with educational technology have shown that tools developed externally, without educator input, often fail to meet the diverse and evolving needs of students and instructors. With GenAI, the opportunity now exists for educators to create personalized materials, assessments, scaffolds, and tutors aligned with their learning objectives. However, risks related to bias, oversimplification, misinformation, and data privacy remain significant—particularly when relying on commercial platforms governed by proprietary models and changing terms of service. To address these risks, Arizona State University has developed the CreateAI platform: a secure, model-agnostic environment built within the university’s infrastructure. CreateAI supports over 40 large language models and allows users to compare, build or customize, and deploy tools without sharing data externally. Educators can co-design AI companions and learning experiences tailored to their students, with embedded ethical safeguards and institutional alignment. Title: Demystify the Role of Memory in Machine Learning Engineering Agents
Source title: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
Abstract: While memory is a core component in agent systems, its behavioral impact in complex, long-horizon domains like machine learning engineering (MLE) remains poorly understood. Unlike short, reactive exchanges, MLE agents solve tasks through cycles of experimentation and improvement where past errors can inform future success. This paper presents a systematic study dissecting how memory influences agent behavior and performance across diverse MLE challenges. We first introduce a dynamic coding memory designed to capture and reuse debugging experiences, and integrate it into two representative agent paradigms: a sequential, chain-based agent that mirrors human-like iterative refinement, and a parallel, tree-based agent that performs broad, self-exploratory search in the code space. Our central finding is that the role of memory is contingent on the agent’s underlying architecture. For chain-based agents, memory proves highly beneficial, enabling them to avoid recurring mistakes and engage in more coherent, iterative refinement, which significantly improves reliability and task success. In contrast, for tree-based search agents, memory introduces a critical trade-off: it enhances procedural stability at the cost of constraining search diversity, which can prematurely narrow exploration and lead to suboptimal final solutions. These findings reveal a fundamental trade-off between procedural reliability and solution innovation modulated by memory, offering insights for designing more effective and robust MLE agents. © 2026 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Authors: Kılıç A.; Hendek M.; Uslu D.
Title: Bibliometric analysis of artificial intelligence applications in food quality control and safety
Source title: Ukrainian Food Journal
Abstract: Introduction. Food safety remains a critical global challenge due to risks associated with food production, processing, packaging, and distribution. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool for improving food quality control and safety through intelligent monitoring, traceability, and decision-making across the food supply chain. Materials and methods. A bibliometric analysis was conducted to evaluate AI applications in food quality control and safety. Data were collected from the Web of Science database using the query "Food*" AND "Safety" AND "Quality Control" AND "Artificial Intelligence", without restrictions on publication year, language, or document type. The retrieved records were analyzed to identify publication trends and key research themes. Results and discussion. The results were organized into two sections: Descriptive Findings and Content Analysis. Data retrieved from the Web of Science (WoS) database were analyzed using the Bibliometrix software package. The publication period spanned 2008-2025 and showed a steady increase in research interest in the application of artificial intelligence (AI) to food quality control and safety, with the highest number of publications recorded in 2025. Following the screening process, 70 relevant studies were included in the analysis. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identified the most frequent terms as "Artificial Intelligence," "Food Safety," "Machine Learning," "Quality," "Quality Control," and "Computer Vision," highlighting the growing role of AI technologies in food safety and quality assessment. The findings also indicate increasing adoption of machine learning, data analytics, and computer vision in food industry applications. Content analysis revealed five major research themes: food analysis, food supply chain management, food traceability, food quality monitoring and management, and food fraud prevention. These themes demonstrate the broad applicability of AI for improving food quality, safety, transparency, and sustainability throughout the food system. Conclusions. The review demonstrates that AI is increasingly being integrated with technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and blockchain to enable real-time monitoring and improve traceability. However, most current applications remain focused on analytical support rather than fully autonomous systems. Future research should prioritize multimodal data fusion and the implementation of explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to enhance predictive performance, transparency, and user trust. © 2026, National University of Food Technologies. Title: Challenges and Opportunities in AI-Human Collaborative Teaching
Source title: Ethical, Legal, and Pedagogical Perspectives on AI in Education
Abstract: This chapter highlights the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in education, focusing on its impact on teaching methodologies, assessment strategies, and student engagement. AI-driven adaptive learning platforms personalize education by analyzing student performance and tailoring content to individual needs. Additionally, AI assists educators by automating administrative tasks, enabling datadriven instruction, and identifying learning gaps. However, ethical concerns such as bias in AI algorithms, student data privacy, and transparency in AI decision-making must be addressed. The chapter also explores compliance with legal frameworks, including the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act (FERPA), and intellectual property laws, which are crucial for ensuring responsible AI use in education. The legal complexities surrounding AI-generated content ownership and liability in AI malfunctions further necessitate the establishment of clear policies and risk management strategies. Moreover, AI’s integration requires pedagogical adaptations, ensuring that AI complements human instruction rather than replacing it. Blended learning models, AI-augmented teacher roles, and gamified learning environments are examined as strategies to promote student-centered education while preserving the essential human connection in teaching. To fully harness AI’s potential; institutions must adopt ethical guidelines, provide professional development for educators, and establish regulatory measures that balance innovation with accountability. © 2026 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Title: SemiXAI-Net: XAI-driven semi-supervised object detection via iterative pseudo-label refinement and spatiotemporal consistency
Source title: PeerJ Computer Science
Abstract: In recent years, object detection has become an indispensable component in various critical applications, ranging from autonomous driving to surveillance systems. However, achieving high detection accuracy alone is insufficient; models must also be transparent and interpretable to foster trust and ensure reliable decision-making, especially in safety-critical domains. Traditional supervised approaches require large amounts of labeled data, which is often expensive and time-consuming to obtain. Additionally, these models typically function as “black boxes,” providing limited insight into their decision processes. This article introduces SemiXAI-Net, a semi-supervised learning framework optimized for object detection tasks while incorporating explainable AI (XAI) techniques to enhance transparency. By utilizing a teacher-student architecture, the framework iteratively refines pseudo-labels, effectively improving both model performance and interpretability. The experimental evaluation was performed using the Common Objects in Context (COCO) dataset (a real-world benchmark) alongside synthetic datasets to simulate semi-supervised conditions. A labeled subset of COCO images was combined with unlabeled data (both from COCO’s unannotated images and synthetic sources) for training. The framework was implemented on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs using PyTorch, with hyperparameters optimized for stability (batch size: 32, learning rate: 0.001) and efficiency. To enable real-time interpretability, the student model integrated Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations (LIME) techniques, generating visual explanations during inference. Training spanned 10 epochs with early stopping to mitigate overfitting risks. SemiXAI-Net achieves a superior accuracy of 93%, precision of 94%, recall of 95%, and an F1-score of 94.5%. In comparison, traditional methods reach a maximum accuracy of 87%. The explainability score of SemiXAI-Net stands at 94%, significantly surpassing the traditional method’s score of 71%. Additionally, the framework demonstrates a generalization ability of 94% on unseen data, making it highly adaptable to new environments. These results highlight SemiXAI-Net’s potential for real-world applications, particularly in critical domains like autonomous driving, where both high performance and model transparency are essential. © Copyright 2026 Tahir et al. Title: AI-driven innovations in higher learning institutions: a review of pre-service teachers’ pedagogical competence through technology integration

Abstract: This study reviews the literature on artificial intelligence (AI)-driven innovations in higher learning institutions with a focus on pre-service teachers’ pedagogical competence through technology integration. It aims to identify how AI-driven tools assist teacher preparation and what opportunities and challenges emerge. Despite growing interest in AI across education, research specifically examining pre-service teachers’ pedagogical competence in higher education contexts remains limited. This study reviewed literature published between 2015 and 2025, sourced from five databases: Google Scholar, PsycINFO, ERIC, SCOPUS, and Web of Science. Key findings identify six AI tools used in teacher education, including adaptive learning systems, VR/AR simulations, generative AI (ChatGPT, DeepSeek), and learning analytics. The study also highlights several gaps in the field, including a lack of longitudinal studies, limited cross-cultural research, insufficient attention to ethical and data privacy concerns, and inadequate AI literacy among pre-service teachers. The proposed Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK)-AI competency framework offers a three-tiered developmental progression, foundational literacy, applied pedagogical integration, and professional AI fluency, to guide curriculum design for AI-enhanced teacher preparation. Title: A Hybrid Bio-Inspired Feature Selection and 3-Tier Ensemble Framework for Explainable Student Performance Prediction in E-Learning
Source title: Proceedings of the 6th International Conference on Trends in Material Science and Inventive Materials, ICTMIM 2026
Abstract: The high rates of development of digital learning settings have heightened the need of having consistent, resilient, and decipherable models that can predict the performance of the students. In this paper, we present a strictly designed, multilevel architecture that is used to classify e-learning performance, which includes preprocessing of the data systematically, a hybrid and bio-inspired feature selection, a three-level ensemble learning architecture, Bayesian hyperparameter optimization, and SHAP-based explainability. The data is the product of the Kalboard 360 Learning Management System and is publicly available in Kaggle and consists of 480 student records, which encompass demographic, academic, and behavioral attributes, which are grouped into three levels of performance. The data preprocessing includes mean-based imputation of missing data, outliers, and the use of the Interquartile Range (IQR) to detect outliers, Synthetic Minority Over-Sampling Technique (SMOTE) to address class imbalance. The feature selection is carried out using a Bio-Inspired BeeWhale Optimization Model, which is the combination of the Artificial Bee Colony and the Whale Optimization algorithm, with the synergy effect, thus selecting the best subset of the predictive features that is relevant. The central predictive algorithm uses a three-layer stacking ensemble based on a Light Gradient Boosting Machine, an Extra Trees Classifier, and a Histogram-Based Gradient Boosting model, and the Light Gradient Boosting Machine is the meta-learner optimized using Bayesian hyperparameter tuning. Empirical experiments show better classification accuracy, which is 98.77, and the area under the ROC curve (AUC) is 0.993. The SHAP analysis of interpretability suggests that the engagement-related features, especially the amount of student absence days and resource usage measures, have the greatest impact on predicting performance. The given framework is very balanced in terms of predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, and transparency, and may be considered highly appropriate to the intelligent e-learning analytics and early intervention systems. © 2026 IEEE.

Authors: Robinson D.H.

Title: Is Generative AI the Latest Educational Technology Innovation “Flavor-of-the-Month”?
Source title: Handbook of Generative AI in Education: Integrating Research into Practice
Abstract: In this chapter, I examine whether generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is truly a transformative force in education or simply the latest in a long line of overhyped technologies. Following Mayer (Psychology of learning and motivation. Academic Press, 2002), I situate GAI within a century of educational technology promises (e.g., film, radio, television, computers, massive open online courses (MOOCs), and learning analytics) that would revolutionize education, only to disappoint when adopted in technology-centered rather than learner-centered ways. GAI, like earlier tools, excels at management: automating routine academic tasks, streamlining editorial workflows, and easing instructional logistics. These affordances can free time for higher-level work, but they also risk diminishing engagement and the intrinsic cognitive effort essential for deep learning. There are also serious concerns associated with GAI, including misinformation, deepfakes, academic dishonesty, and the potential erosion of critical thinking and human interaction. I argue that, to move beyond “flavor-of-the-month” status, GAI must be pedagogically aligned—supporting individualized, optimally challenging, feedback-rich learning experiences—and its use must be evaluated with rigorous intervention research that measures actual learning, not just satisfaction. Without such evidence, GAI is unlikely to escape the fate of prior educational technology fads. © The Editor(s) (if applicable) and The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Beyond Automation: A Systematic Review of AI Teaching Methodologies and a Framework for Human-AI Synergy in Higher Education
Source title: IEEE Access
Abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly present in educational settings, yet its integration remains fragmented, lacking coherent understanding of how teachers and AI can effectively collaborate. This systematic review of 169 peer-reviewed studies (2009-2024) introduces the AI-Human Synergy Framework, a model for categorizing educational AI based on autonomy and collaboration, empirically validated through systematic coding with exceptional inter-rater reliability (κ = 0.972). Our analysis reveals significant automation bias: 45.56% of implementations substitute human functions, while only 4.73% achieve genuine human-AI partnership - a 10:1 ratio. Through rigorous analysis across diverse AI methods - from Predictive Analytics to Generative AI - we demonstrate that educators are predominantly positioned as data interpreters rather than collaborative partners. While recent work (2023-2024) shows promising shifts toward Augmentation (62.5%), true Synergy remains critically underrepresented. This framework provides the first empirical quantification of the substitution-synergy gap and offers actionable implementation tools, underscoring the urgent need to prioritize collaborative design over automation as Generative AI reshapes educational practice.  © 2013 IEEE.

Title: Video Interaction-Enhanced Knowledge Tracing based on Heterogeneous Graphs with Temporal Modeling in E-learning Environments
Source title: Proceedings of the International Conference on Computer Supported Cooperative Work in Design, CSCWD
Abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) aims to model and predict students' knowledge states from their historical learning behaviors. With the development of e-learning platforms, large amounts of fine-grained learning behavior data, such as video interaction data and answer records, have been collected. However, existing KT models still mainly rely on answer records and fail to effectively incorporate video interaction data, which limits the accuracy of knowledge state modeling and tracing. To address this limitation, we propose a video interaction-enhanced KT model based on heterogeneous graphs with temporal modeling, denoted as VIKT-HGTM. This model constructs a heterogeneous graph integrating students, videos, exercises, and knowledge concepts, and defines meta-paths to capture semantic relationships among these entities. To capture dynamic changes in learning behavior, VIKT-HGTM employs an attention-based fusion mechanism to aggregate information from different metapaths and incorporates a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to perform temporal encoding of meta-path features. Furthermore, the model introduces meta-path-aware contrastive learning to enhance the consistency and discriminability of temporal representations. Experiments conducted on a real-world dataset show that VIKT-HGTM can effectively improve KT performance. Specifically, on the answer prediction task, it achieves improvements of 3.86% in AUC, 3.67% in ACC and 3.04% in RMSE compared with existing models. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: BloomAgent: An Agentic AI System for Outcome-Based Course Delivery and Curriculum Intelligence
Source title: Agentic AI and the Intelligent Transformation of Higher Education
Abstract: A persistent compounding challenge faces higher education institutions operating under Outcome-Based Education (OBE) frameworks: faculty must concurrently create curricula that are in line with Programme Outcomes (POs) create assessments that accurately target the intended cognitive levels specified by the Revised Blooms Taxonomy (RBT) produce attainment evidence that is ready for accreditation and continuously improve their courses based on student performance data. Without comprehensive institutional support these demands coexist and result in systemic inconsistencies in outcome attainment reporting curriculum quality and assessment validity. This chapter describes BloomAgent a purpose-built agentic AI system that tackles these issues through four interrelated operational layers: (1) a CO-PO Alignment Auditor that assesses and improves the mapping between Course Outcomes and Programme Outcomes prior to the start of delivery (2) an Instructional Strategy Advisor that suggests pedagogically grounded approaches calibrated to the cognitive demands of each stated learning outcome (3) an Assessment Co-Designer that creates assessment tools rubrics and Tables of Specifications that are specifically mapped to RBT levels and the corresponding COs and (4) a Curriculum Intelligence Engine that converts end-of-cycle performance data into actionable revision recommendations and reports that are ready for accreditation. The chapter synthesizes OBE compliance theory RBT frameworks and agentic AI architectures to develop BloomAgents theoretical underpinnings. It offers a scalable deployment model CO-PO mapping mechanisms and a comprehensive system architecture across three institutional tiers ranging from research-intensive universities to teaching colleges with limited resources. This chapter argues that responsible governance architecture is inextricably linked to technical design and critically examines a comprehensive ethical and governance framework that addresses algorithmic bias faculty academic freedom student data privacy and institutional accountability. BloomAgent is positioned as an intelligent partner that expands faculty capacity while upholding institutional accountability for educational quality rather than as a substitute for expert pedagogical judgment. © 2027 by IGI Global Scientific Publishing. Abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into educational contexts has intensified concerns regarding transparency, accountability, fairness, and stakeholder agency. Explainable AI (XAI) research has the potential to advance methods for interpreting complex machine learning models, revealing opportunities to utilize explainability to enable safe, sustainable, and user-driven implementation of AI-supported systems in authentic educational settings. This half-day interdisciplinary workshop addresses this potential by focusing on explainability by design as a mechanism for strengthening the agency of teachers, learners, and institutions. Bringing together researchers and practitioners from AIED, EDM, and L@S, we aim to develop a shared understanding of design principles, XAI frameworks, technical challenges, and a research agenda for embedding transparency across the entire AI life cycle, from data pipelines and modeling to classroom integration and governance. We utilize targeted discussions, engaging talks and group activities to emphasize collaborative and cross-disciplinary exchange and long-term community building. Title: Designing ChatGPT-mediated feedback activities in EFL writing: a design-based study of the dialogic feedback triangle
Source title: Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education
Abstract: With the rise of GenAI-assisted English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing, chatbots such as ChatGPT have shown potential both as formative feedback providers and interactive partners, offering new possibilities for dialogic feedback. However, little research has explored how educational practitioners can design and implement ChatGPT-mediated dialogic feedback activities. Addressing this gap, this study adopted a design-based research (DBR) approach to iteratively develop an optimal design for ChatGPT-mediated dialogic feedback activities, drawing on a dialogic feedback triangle as a conceptual framework. Across three iterative cycles with four EFL learners, data were collected through semi-structured observations and interviews focused on participants’ writing experiences and feedback on the intervention. The three research rounds led to the identification of seven key design elements, organised into a three-dimensional feedback triangle: cognitive (disciplinary knowledge, cue-consciousness, self-evaluation), socio-affective (adaptive roles of ChatGPT at different writing stages, learners’ critical attitudes towards ChatGPT), and structural (mobilisation of learners’ tool repertoires, feedback structures based on specific formats and standards). These design elements can offer insights into feedback literacy and inform seven practical deisign principles to guide educators and technology designers in designing and implementing effective GenAI-mediated dialogic feedback experiences in EFL writing contexts. © 2025 The Author(s). Title: Artificial Intelligence in Inclusive and Special Education: A Narrative Survey
Source title: International Journal of Special Education
Abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly discussed as a means of supporting inclusive and special education through adaptive learning, assistive technologies, learning analytics, automated feedback, and generative AI. However, the educational value of AI for learners with disabilities depends on accessibility, pedagogical alignment, data protection, teacher agency, and equitable implementation. Objectives: This narrative survey synthesizes current literature and policy guidance on AI in inclusive and special education, with emphasis on applications, opportunities, risks, and responsible implementation. Methods: The paper uses a structured narrative review approach based on peer-reviewed review articles, foundational AI-in-education literature, and international policy sources relevant to inclusive education, assistive technology, and AI governance. Results: The synthesis indicates that AI may support personalization, accessibility, communication, teacher workload reduction, early identification of support needs, and formative feedback. At the same time, evidence remains uneven across disability groups, educational levels, and low-resource contexts. Major risks include inaccurate outputs, bias, privacy concerns, limited transparency, over-reliance, insufficient teacher preparation, and inequitable access. Conclusion: AI should be positioned as a human-supervised support system rather than a substitute for teachers, special educators, therapists, or institutional responsibility. Responsible adoption requires Universal Design for Learning, learner and family participation, rigorous evaluation, transparent policies, and safeguards for privacy, fairness, and academic integrity. © 2026 Authors.

Title: AI for All: An Open Agentic Framework for Predictive, Preventive, and Ethical Learning Analytics in Higher Education
Source title: 8th International Conference on Activity and Behavior Computing, ABC 2026
Abstract: Student dropout remains a persistent challenge in higher education, with substantial academic, social, and economic consequences. Although AI-driven learning analytics have shown promise in identifying at-risk students, many existing approaches suffer from limited interpretability, high deployment costs, and weak alignment with educational theory. To address these gaps, this study presents the Open Agentic Predictive Preventive Ethical (OAPPE) Framework, a fully open-source, lowcode architecture that integrates interpretable machine learning with agentic AI-driven automation for dropout prediction and prevention. The framework integrates principles from Self-Determination Theory and Constructivist Learning Theory to support proactive, student-centered interventions that promote autonomy, competence, and relatedness. OAPPE is implemented and evaluated using an open educational dataset from the University of California, Irvine Machine Learning Repository, with the predictive pipeline implemented using LightGBM and SHAPbased explanations in a fully reproducible, cost-free environment using Google Colab and n8n. Empirical results demonstrate robust predictive performance with a mean AUC of 0.82 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.71, while the agentic workflow attains a 91 percent trigger success rate and high ethical transparency, evidenced by an expert interpretability rating of 4.6 out of 5. Overall, the findings demonstrate that interpretable, ethically aligned, and scalable agentic AI systems for learning analytics can be realized using open technologies, positioning OAPPE as a human-centered blueprint for student retention in higher education. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: SGAASS: A Closed-Loop Adaptive Framework for Personalized Skill Gap Analysis and Deadline-Aware Study Scheduling using NLP

Abstract: The fast-changing developments in industries present a new challenge by leaving learners' ability to meet the expectations of employers. Hence, available educational platforms keep providing learning materials that are based more on the general popularity of specific subjects than on assessing the skills lacking for fulfilling a specific job role. As opposed to traditional recommending platforms, APS continually adjusts priorities using combined data on the level of skill gaps, learner's success in mastering required skills, learning speed, and urgency of deadlines and the cold start problem according to the approach of gradient-free optimization. This framework utilizes only standard CPU hardware without necessitating the use of large language models or GPU processing, thereby guaranteeing effective deployment and computational efficiency. Title: Predicting the Reliability of Students in Using Artificial Intelligence for Academic Writing Using Machine Learning Techniques
Source title: Proceedings of 3rd International Conference on Machine Learning and Autonomous Systems, ICMLAS 2026
Abstract: The increasing integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic writing has raised critical concerns regarding students' reliability, ethical responsibility, and verification practices. While existing studies largely emphasize attitudes and self-reported perceptions toward AI use, limited research has examined academic reliability as a measurable, behavior-driven construct. This study proposes a multidimensional framework for modeling students' reliability in AI-assisted academic writing by integrating five key constructs: AI usage intensity, verification practices, ethical reliability, AI literacy, and performance behavior. Using survey data from undergraduate students, these constructs were transformed into engineered features and employed in supervised machine learning classification to predict students' reliability levels categorized as low, moderate, and high. Three models were evaluated: Support Vector Machine (SVM), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and a lightweight tabular Deep Neural Network (DNN). Results indicate that classical machine learning approaches significantly outperform deep learning in this context, with both SVM and KNN achieving an accuracy of 91.67%, supported by balanced precision, recall, and F1-scores across all classes. In contrast, the lightweight DNN demonstrated limited effectiveness, achieving only 32.50% accuracy, highlighting the importance of model-data compatibility in educational analytics. The findings suggest that students' academic reliability in AI-assisted writing is best captured through interpretable, proximity-based, and margin-based learning frameworks, rather than complex deep architectures. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: AI-Enabled Vocabulary Learning with Adaptive Scheduling and Chatbot Practice: Toward Lexical Network Aware Modeling

Abstract: Vocabulary mastery underpins reading comprehension, listening ability and overall second language proficiency, yet many learners still rely on one size fits all drills that ignore both individual forgetting curves and the lexical interdependencies that shape real word networks. Recent work on spaced repetition and knowledge tracing offers a means to adapt review schedules based on learner responses, but most implementations treat each word as an isolated skill. This paper presents an AI enabled vocabulary learning system that couples knowledge tracing with a lexical network aware item representation, a utility based scheduler with explicit parameter settings, and a conversational practice module enhanced with gamified micro challenges. Unlike prior synthetic benchmarks, our simulation incorporates fatigue, off task behaviour and random guessing to approximate noisier real world usage. Results from the Monte Carlo evaluation indicate that, under the stated simulation assumptions, the integrated adaptive condition yields higher expected vocabulary gains and engagement efficiency than the fixed interval baseline. The simulations also suggest that explicitly modelling semantic and morphological relationships can reduce interference and support associative reinforcement. Title: Counterfactual Grade Prediction: Disentangling Peer Effects and Environmental Bias via Causal Graph Attention Networks
Source title: 2026 15th International Conference on Educational and Information Technology, ICEIT 2026
Abstract: Precision prediction of academic performance is increasingly used in precision intervention in the high school period, especially in the environment of resource misallocation led by the pressure of the college entrance examination. However, in realistic small-cohort settings (e.g., N ≈ 100), conventional regression and sequential models can be unstable, overlook peer effects driven by social homophily, and inadvertently amplify environmental bias by over-weighting socioeconomic proxies such as residential address. These shortages directly threaten the educational fairness that students could be marked as "at-risk"by environmental effects, rather than non-learnable and non-intervenable factors. We introduce the Causal-GAT applied in counterfactual grade prediction. This method can divide the peer effects from the complex environmental effects. Causal-GAT constructs a heterogeneous student graph, establishing individual associations by residential proximity, co-enrollment in elective courses, and behavioral similarity signals. To avoid false relevance, we employ a causal structure learning mechanism that sends the message only in situations where there may be a causal relationship, by pruning noisy edges. In addition to the predictive function, based on the learned causal relationship, we make causal relationships and answer "hypothetical"questions. For instance, will the risk of student failure change when peer support improves? This framework enhances robustness in small-data scenarios, applies explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) based on the causal paths, and provides actionable and equity-aware insights for school decision-making.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: STUDENT DROPOUT PREDICTION IN HIGHER EDUCATION: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF MACHINE LEARNING METHODS AND RISK FACTORS
Source title: Journal of Information Technology Education: Research
Abstract: Aim/Purpose This study systematically reviews machine learning techniques for predicting undergraduate student dropout in higher education, identifies related risk factors, explores methodological gaps in Machine Learning (ML)-based dropout prediction, and outlines directions for future research and institutional implementation. Background Student dropout remains a persistent global challenge with significant academic and socioeconomic implications. Although many studies report high predictive accuracy for dropout models, there is still limited understanding of how these models operationalize educational theory, incorporate psychosocial and equity-related factors, and translate predictions into empirically validated interventions in real institutional settings. Methodology The review followed Kitchenham’s methodology and PRISMA 2020 guidelines, using a PICO-C framework focused on undergraduate higher education. Searches from 2019 to 2024 across eight databases yielded 301 records. After screening using predefined inclusion/exclusion criteria, double review with Cohen’s kappa, and a 16-criterion weighted quality assessment (including automated keyword checks), 75 studies met all quality and relevance thresholds. Contribution This systematic review synthesizes 75 quality-assessed studies on ML-based undergraduate dropout prediction, clarifying which algorithms currently dominate the field, which risk factors and theoretical frameworks are most frequently used, and where critical gaps remain in generalizability, equity, explainability, temporal modeling, and intervention validation. It is distinctive for its explicit quality-weighting process, its focus on the actionability gap, and its mapping of emerging trends and outstanding needs in the field. Findings The systematic review shows rapid growth in dropout prediction research from 2019 to 2024, reflecting increased institutional awareness. Academic performance and engagement indicators are the most used risk factors in prediction models, whereas psychosocial factors (including self-efficacy, sense of belonging, motivation, and resilience) remain significantly underrepresented. Ensemble methods (particularly Random Forest and XGBoost) dominate the algorithm landscape, consistently achieving accuracies of around 86–88%. However, most studies rely on single-institution datasets, do not account for temporal changes, and rarely evaluate the impact or fairness of interventions triggered by predictions. These limitations reduce the generalizability, equity, and practical utility of ML-based predictive models in higher education. Recommendations Machine learning models should be viewed as decision-support tools, not for Practitioners standalone solutions. By combining predictive risk assessments with academic, financial, and engagement data, institutions can design multi-dimensional retention strategies, implement early-stage monitoring protocols, and establish clear intervention procedures that are evaluated for effectiveness and fairness. Recommendations Researchers should move beyond single-institution, static models toward longifor Researchers tudinal, cross-institutional designs that incorporate temporal dynamics, transfer learning, and domain adaptation. Future studies should integrate psychosocial, motivational, and equity-oriented variables; systematically apply fairness-aware machine learning and explainability (XAI) techniques; and empirically evaluate whether predictive systems improve retention through controlled intervention studies. Impact on Society By clarifying how machine learning can reliably identify students at risk of dropout and exposing current limitations in fairness and implementation, this review supports the design of more equitable and effective retention policies in higher education. Improved early-warning systems and evidence-based interventions can reduce economic losses, mitigate social inequality, and enhance graduation rates, particularly in regions with historically high attrition. Future Research Future research should focus on cross-institutional benchmark datasets, longitudinal cohort studies, and models that adapt to diverse institutional and regional contexts. There is a pressing need for studies that integrate psychosocial and structural factors, evaluate fairness across vulnerable groups, apply explainability frameworks as standard practice, and link predictive models to experimentally tested intervention strategies, moving the field from predictive accuracy toward demonstrable educational impact. Abstract: This chapter examines the integration of artificial intelligence in higher education, arguing that AI should function as a collaborative partner that amplifies human creativity rather than replacing it. Drawing on learning analytics, student narratives, and current research, it introduces an original three-model framework of human-AI collaboration complementary, iterative, and augmentative grounded in creativity theory and specifying the conditions under which each model is most appropriate. Title: EduAdapt: AI based Personalized Learning and Tutoring System
Source title: 6th International Conference on Computer Networks and Inventive Communication Technologies, ICCNCT 2026 - Proceedings
Abstract: Personalized learning is increasingly important because learners differ in prior knowledge, pace, and learning preferences, which are not adequately supported by traditional one-size-fits-all instruction. This paper presents a full-stack AI-powered personalized learning platform designed to provide adaptive, learner-centric support through continuous analysis of learner activity. The system is built with a React frontend, a FastAPI backend, and a MongoDB data layer, enabling secure user management, scalable content handling, and real-time interaction. It uses learner profile attributes, quiz performance, document uploads, and chat history to drive personalization. A topic-level mastery modeling pipeline and machine learning-based recommendation engine are used to detect weak areas and prioritize next learning objectives. To support contextual tutoring, the platform integrates document-aware retrieval and large language model-based response generation, allowing learners to ask questions and receive targeted explanations grounded in uploaded study material. The system also includes adaptive quiz generation, weekly roadmap creation, study planning, and analytics dashboards to track progress over time. By combining adaptive recommendation, intelligent tutoring, and performance monitoring in a unified architecture, the proposed platform offers a practical and extensible framework for personalized education in modern digital learning environments. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Assessment validity in the age of generative artificial intelligence: a critical review
Source title: Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education
Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents significant challenges to assessment validity in higher education. In response, universities worldwide have invested heavily in risk-mitigation strategies. However, such efforts often prove insufficient given the rapid and on-going development of GenAI capabilities, prompting sustained debate about how assessment in higher education can remain valid in this evolving landscape. At the same time, inconsistencies in assessment design and implementation have raised concerns regarding the assurance of learning. This study presents a critical review of the literature on assessment validity in the context of GenAI through a discourse-analytic examination of articles published in 10 leading higher education journals between 2023 and June 2025. Articles were selected using predefined inclusion criteria, and discourse analysis was employed to synthesise dominant narratives within the literature. Three main discourses were identified: (1) risk-oriented framings that emphasise academic integrity breaches, (2) rule-based approaches centred on detection and policy enforcement, and (3) design-focused approaches that advocate resilient assessment redesign. The findings offer conceptual and practical implications for assessment practice and institutional policy in higher education in the age of GenAI. © 2026 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group.

Title: Beyond Student Outputs: Design Requirements for Teacher-Facing Process Analytics in AI-Assisted Block-Based Programming
Source title: IEEE Transactions on Learning Technologies
Abstract: This article reports an early stage requirement and interpretability study of teacher-facing process analytics for artificial intelligence (AI)-Assisted block-based programming. The study elicited teachers' judgments about what process evidence, report elements, and guardrail conditions would be needed when students may consult external generative AI while solving Entry-based tasks. An online survey of 312 current elementary teachers in Daegu Metropolitan City and Gyeongsangbuk-do, South Korea, was analyzed using descriptive statistics, readability-usefulness mapping, exploratory regression analyses, and inductive thematic analysis. Teachers strongly endorsed the need for process evidence beyond final products. Across all five candidate evidence types, mean perceived instructional usefulness was descriptively higher than mean conceptual readability, indicating that several signals were valued for classroom judgment while requiring interpretive support. Teachers also prioritized one-page summaries, visible evidence, plain-language wording, and brief intervention cues, together with editable interpretations, uncertainty cues, nonlabeling language, and clear privacy rules. The findings provide survey-grounded early stage design requirements for teacher-facing analytics by identifying candidate process-evidence types, capture-To-report translation needs, and guardrail conditions that support evidence-linked, revisable summaries under teacher judgment.  © 2008-2011 IEEE.

Title: Simulation of Competence-Based Difficulty Adjustment in Formal-Language Exercises
Source title: International Conference on Computer Supported Education, CSEDU - Proceedings
Abstract: Understanding, applying, and evaluating formal languages are key competences in many technical and scientific professions. This is true despite, and especially because of, the ability of generative AI to generate artifacts of formal languages, such as source code or mathematical notation. Acquiring competences generally requires targeted practice. Adaptive learning systems use knowledge tracing (KT) models to guide learners toward learning success in a targeted manner-at least in theory. In order to increase the practicality of adaptive learning systems, large amounts of data are usually required, but collecting this data is very time-consuming and expensive. This paper presents a model for developing learners’ formal language competences by working on exercises of increasing complexity and implements this model in a simulation. Based on the data obtained from the simulation, a KT model is trained and its application is then evaluated in the simulation. The results show that the KT model is well suited for application in the simulation. However, the competence development model requires further evaluation based on real data in order to confirm the validity of the model assumptions and to further develop the latter. Title: A Dialogue-Based Learning Analytics Framework for Collaborative Game-Based Learning

Abstract: In computer-supported collaborative learning environments, analyzing student dialogue is essential for understanding collaborative problem-solving behaviors and supporting effective learning. Prior work often treats all dialogue interactions uniformly, failing to capture how specific dialogue interaction differentially impact learning experiences and outcomes. To address this limitation, we introduce a dialogue-based learning analytics framework that integrates weighted temporal clustering of dialogue with large language model-based interpretation. Our framework identifies student interaction patterns most predictive of group learning gains and uses these insights to enable early prediction of learning outcomes and generate pedagogically meaningful interpretations. In addition, expert evaluations and case studies demonstrate that the identified weighted dialogue patterns reflect key collaborative problem-solving behaviors recognized as important in collaborative learning. Abstract: The integration of AI into the educational system is especially innovative on the subcontinent of India and its surrounding areas. This chapter focuses on the incorporation of AI tools into higher education, the addition of AI tools into startups, the skill formation AI tools help develop, and the controversies surrounding them. Adopting a case study approach, we look at policy documents; interview transcripts from academics, students, and entrepreneurs; and fieldwork observations from incubation centers and hackathon events. While surveys provide overarching usage trends (Adhikari & Gope, 2025; Kumar et al., 2025), case studies provide a deeper, finer understanding of the practices, resistance, and contextual blockages that emerge. The remainder of the analysis highlights three broad insights. First, the integration of AI into assessment and learning analytics (Yan et al., 2023), particularly in higher education, remains a work in progress. Discrimination in funding and resource allocation continues to exist (Suri, 2025). Additionally, the AI skill-development programs highlighted the gaps in infrastructure and the unwillingness of the faculty to embrace technology (Goyal et al., 2025). To ground these changes in business reality, we have integrated three platform-centered case studies with Pega GenAI: Intelligent Claims Processing in Health Insurance, AI-Augmented Care Management in Healthcare, and AI-Assisted Loan Origination in Finance. In these case studies, the routine document intake, triage, and summarization workflows, as well as other generative and prescriptive processes, are enhanced and streamlined. They surface automatable explainable decisions and compliance with human supervision. The benefits are faster cycle times, lower operational costs, better auditability, and increased risk of exposure to data fairness, privacy, trust, and clinician/analyst attention. Title: A Hybrid Machine Learning and Explainable Analytics Framework for Predicting and Monitoring Student Academic Performance
Source title: Proceedings of 8th International Conference on Intelligent Sustainable Systems, ICISS 2026
Abstract: Accurate prediction of student academic performance is essential for enabling early academic interventions and supporting institutional decision-making. However, most existing educational analytics approaches are retrospective in nature, rely on categorical performance classification, or employ single predictive models with limited optimisation and interpretability. To address these limitations, this work presents a hybrid machine learning and explainable analytics framework for predicting Grade Point Average (GPA) on a 10-point scale. The proposed approach integrates traditional machine learning techniques, ensemble models, and deep learning methods to analyse both academic and behavioural attributes. A dataset comprising 2,000 student records is used, including attendance, study habits, sleep duration, stress levels, physical activity, and extracurricular participation. Five predictive models-Decision Tree, Random Forest, Grid Search-optimised Random Forest, XGBoost, and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-are developed and systematically evaluated using standard regression metrics. Experimental results indicate that the Grid Search-optimised Random Forest model achieves the best predictive performance, with an R- value of 0.80, a Mean Absolute Error of 0.09, and a Root Mean Square Error of 0.10. Feature importance analysis further reveals that attendance, study hours, and sleep duration are the most influential factors affecting GPA, providing interpretable insights into student performance. In addition, the framework supports real-time academic monitoring through a modular visualisation dashboard and a recommendation chatbot that delivers personalised academic guidance. Overall, the results show that combining behavioural analytics with optimised ensemble models lead to an accurate, interpretable, and practically deployable solution for student performance prediction. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: A HYBRID MODEL BASED ON MACHINE LEARNING AND GENERATIVE AI FOR PREDICTING ACADEMIC PERFORMANCE FROM LEARNING TRACES

Abstract: The analysis of students' learning traces in digital environments enables a better understanding of the factors influencing their academic performance. This paper proposes a hybrid predictive model combining Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to predict students' academic performance (GPA) by leveraging traces from six dimensions: demographic, cognitive, social, emotional, contextual, and normative. First, the Random Forest algorithm is used to select the most relevant features. Then, a combined model based on MLP, LSTM, and XGBoost is trained to optimize prediction accuracy. Generative AI (DeepSeek) is integrated to enrich contextual data and provide personalized recommendations. Model decisions are interpreted using SHAP, allowing for explainability of the predictions. The model is evaluated on a real dataset of 1,002,393 records, built from learning traces collected from student interactions with courses hosted on a Moodle platform. The results highlight a significant improvement in predictive performance (a coefficient of determination of 87%, an average precision of 89.2%, an overall recall of 87.5%, an F1-score of 88.3%, and an accuracy of 90.4%) compared to traditional approaches. This work underscores the value of hybrid techniques for advanced educational data analysis.
