Title: PRIVACY-ADAPTIVE GENERATIVE AI: FROM UNSTRUCTURED REPORTS TO COMPETENCY-BASED LEARNING ANALYTICS
Source title: Proceedings of the International CDIO Conference
Abstract: Background: Challenge-Based Learning (CBL) courses generate a wealth of unstructured student artifacts (e.g., reports, prototypes) that contain rich evidence of professional competencies (CDIO Standard 11). However, extracting these process variables for longitudinal analysis has historically required prohibitive manual effort, leaving valuable curriculum insights inaccessible. As a result, assessment practices often rely on coarse indicators (e.g., grades), limiting evidence-based feedback on innovation and professional skills. Challenge: While Generative AI offers a scalable solution to automate this extraction, institutions face a dilemma: utilizing frontier cloud models risks violating data sovereignty regulations, while privacy-preserving local models have historically lacked the reasoning capability required for complex assessment. Methodology: This paper presents a Privacy-Adaptive Dual-Pipeline framework to resolve this tension. We analyze a subset of 15-year archive of engineering capstone projects (N = 63 validated samples) by benchmarking a local, offline Large Language Model (LLM) against a frontier Cloud model. Results: We identify a distinct Inference Gap: while local models successfully extract explicit identity metadata (Title: 78.2% match), they struggle with semantic reasoning tasks (e.g., Value Proposition: 0.0% match) compared to the cloud benchmark. Contribution: We propose a tiered implementation strategy that allows educators to select the appropriate privacy tier based on data sensitivity. This methodology provides the CDIO community with a validated workflow to transform unstructured repositories into structured datasets, enabling scalable, evidence-based assessment and feedback without compromising student privacy. © 2026 22nd International CDIO Conference. Title: iSmart Guide: Transforming Adult Learning with  AI-Powered Personalization

Abstract: The evolution of digital education tools has reshaped learning experiences, particularly for adult learners juggling diverse commitments. This study explores the transformative role of iSmartGuide, an AI-powered educational platform developed by the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS), in addressing the unique needs of this demographic. This study examines the development, applications, and impact of iSmartGuide, highlighting its potential to set new benchmarks in lifelong learning and digital pedagogy. Title: AI-Based Early Learning Difficulty Detection from Student Text
Source title: 2026 International Conference on Natural Language Processing and Computer Vision, ICNPCV 2026
Abstract: Early identification of students with learning difficulties is essential for providing timely instructional support. Although Natural Language Processing (NLP) enables automated analysis of student-written text, most existing models are opaque black boxes, which limits teacher confidence in AI-assisted learning analytics [29], [30]. This paper proposes an Explainable AI (XAI) framework for early learning difficulty detection based on a fine-tuned Hybrid Meta-Classifier that combines a crossencoder BERT architecture with explicit linguistic features. The model was evaluated on 2,208 student responses, achieving a binary classification accuracy of 83.71% and an ROC AUC of 0.90. Although the standalone fine-tuned BERT model achieves a marginally higher raw accuracy (84.84%), the Hybrid Meta-Classifier deliberately trades a small reduction in accuracy for substantially improved interpretability: fusing linguistic features with neural probabilities enables human-readable, token-level diagnostic feedback via SHAP [17], which is essential for educator trust and actionable intervention. Data efficiency was validated through few-shot transfer learning on a separate 4,380-sample reading comprehension dataset, requiring as few as 100 training samples to adapt. An algorithmic fairness analysis [7] and a microservice deployment architecture for Learning Management System (LMS) integration are also presented. These findings indicate that explainable, bias-aware NLP analytics can support actionable early detection of learning difficulties in real classroom settings.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Longitudinal Shifts in Student Peer Feedback Before and During the GenAI Era
Source title: 2026 22nd International Conference on Information Technology Based Higher Education and Training, ITHET 2026
Abstract: Peer review is widely used to scale formative assessment and develop feedback literacy, yet evidence about how student peer feedback evolves over multiple cohorts remains scarce. This paper analyzes a longitudinal corpus of anonymized peer reviews on seminar papers collected across eight annual cohorts (2019-2026). Each student reviewed three peers using a rubric with criterion-level ratings and open comments, plus an overall assessment. We quantify changes in the discourse of peer feedback using reproducible text-based measures (verbosity, lexical diversity, rhetorical markers) and relate these to rating severity and review timing. To examine shifts plausibly associated with widespread adoption of generative AI tools following the public release of ChatGPT in late 2022, we compare a pre-period (2019-2022) with a post-period (2024-2026), treating 2023 as a transition year. Results show a marked increase in criterion-comment length after 2024 (+54% words), a concurrent decrease in lexical diversity, and a rise in summary/conclusion markers (e.g., "insgesamt", "Fazit"). At the same time, criterion grades become slightly more critical. We discuss these shifts as signatures of changing peer-feedback practices in a GenAI era and derive design implications for preserving authenticity and learning value in rubric-based peer assessment.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: AI-Enhanced Science Learning for Primary Students With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Quasi-Experimental Study With Educational Robotics and Virtual Reality
Source title: Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders
Abstract: Purpose: This study examines the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enhanced instructional tools on science learning, engagement, and social interaction among primary school students with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The research addresses a gap in the literature by exploring how adaptive, multisensory technologies can support conceptual understanding of “Light and Color” and foster inclusive learning experiences in special education settings. Methods: A quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design was implemented with 34 students with ASD, divided into an experimental group and a control group receiving traditional teaching. Quantitative data were collected through science knowledge tests, teacher-rated engagement scales, and AI-generated learning analytics. Qualitative data were obtained through structured observations and teacher reflective journals. Statistical analyses included paired t-tests, ANOVA, MANOVA, and effect size calculations, while qualitative data underwent thematic analysis. Results: Students in the AI-enhanced group demonstrated significantly greater improvements in conceptual understanding compared to the control group, with large effect sizes across most test items. Engagement and motivation ratings were also higher for the experimental group. Qualitative observations revealed increased curiosity, sustained attention, collaborative behaviors, emotional regulation, and autonomy when interacting with the robot and VR environments. Conclusion: AI-enhanced, multisensory instruction substantially benefits neurodiverse learners by promoting deeper conceptual learning, supporting emotional and behavioral engagement, and enhancing inclusive participation. Findings highlight the pedagogical value of integrating adaptive AI tools into science education for students with ASD and suggest that AI can serve as an effective co-mediator alongside teachers in special education contexts. © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2026.

Authors: Al-Otaibi M.
Author full names: Al-Otaibi, Mutaib (58687545000)
Title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Applications on University Teaching Quality and Students’ Self-Directed Learning Skills
Source title: Social Science Forum
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) applications are rapidly reshaping university teaching through adaptive tutoring, generative dialogue, automated feedback, learning analytics, predictive support, and AI-assisted assessment. Yet the educational value of these applications depends not merely on access to technology but on how they are embedded in pedagogy. This study examines the impact of AI applications on university teaching quality and students’ self-directed and self-regulated learning skills. It uses a systematic integrative review and a secondary quantitative synthesis of verified, peer-reviewed evidence. The principal quantitative corpus comprises 85 higher-education studies, 387 dependent effect-size estimates, and 9,564 participants published between 2015 and 2025. Descriptive analyses were reconstructed from publicly available supplementary data, while inferential conclusions were based on published three-level and random-effects meta-analytic estimates; no synthetic data were used. AI feedback had a medium positive average effect on self-regulated learning (Hedges’ g = 0.509), but its 95% prediction interval ranged from −0.661 to 1.678, indicating that effects are highly conditional. Generative-AI interventions also improved academic performance (g = 0.683, 95% CI [0.17, 1.19]), while ChatGPT-supported learning improved behavioral, cognitive, and emotional engagement. However, heterogeneity was substantial, AI feedback did not clearly outperform human feedback, and experimental evidence identified risks of dependence, shallow processing, and “metacognitive laziness.” Teacher support emerged as a decisive pedagogical condition in the academic-performance literature: teacher-supported student–AI interaction produced a large effect (g = 1.426), whereas unsupported use produced a near-zero effect (g = 0.077). The study concludes that AI can improve university teaching quality and learner autonomy when it functions as a scaffold within teacher-designed learning, not as a substitute for disciplinary teaching, human feedback, reflective judgment, or independent performance. © 2026 Slovenian Sociological Association. Title: AILitHub: Building AI Literacy Infrastructure to Situate Frameworks into Practice

Abstract: While AI literacy frameworks are becoming more widely adopted, a key gap remains: we still lack practical infrastructure for educators to collect, share, and understand real classroom cases that connect framework ideas to situated teaching practice. Such infrastructure may help strengthen the connection between theory and practice. In this work, we present AILitHub, a multilingual and scalable web system that enables teachers to contribute AI-related educational cases and annotate them with stakeholders and competencies defined in the OECD AI Literacy Framework. We position AILitHub as an early infrastructure for future professional learning and research. It contributes a scalable case-collection mechanism and may provide practice-grounded evidence that can inform future framework refinement and AI education design. In a preliminary deployment within an AI literacy professional training program, we successfully collected 53 complete teacher-contributed cases. Early results suggest that, while teachers showed strength in contributing positive cases demonstrating AI literacy, they may lack the skill or awareness to identify and provide negative examples. © 2026 Copyright for this paper by its authors.

Abstract: The advent of robust, open generative AI systems has changed teaching, learning, and educational technology permanently and in ways that will continue to evolve in the coming years. Title: Multimodal AI in Education: Research Trends and Emerging Pedagogical Applications

Abstract: This paper presents a bibliometric study of the scientific literature on multimodal artificial intelligence (AI) in education, with the objective of comprehending the intellectual landscape, key contributors, and most prominent and emerging themes in this rapidly developing area of scientific inquiry. The search was conducted on the Scopus database using a Boolean search approach that combined search terms on multimodal AI and education, resulting in a final list of 123 documents published between 2015 and 2026. The VOSviewer software application was used to create co-authorship networks at the author, institutional, and country levels, as well as keyword cooccurrence maps, to explore collaboration and thematic dynamics. The results show that scientific publication in this area was surprisingly low until 2022, when it suddenly jumped to almost 70 publications in 2025, which indicates the explosive development of generative and multimodal AI systems. The United States of America and China emerged as the most productive countries, followed by India and the United Kingdom, while the most influential authors were Giannakos, Michail N., Di Mitri, Daniele, and Cukurova, Mutlu. In the theme analysis, it was revealed that the primary research focus is on multimodal learning analytics, educational technology, and large language models, which have the potential to be applied in emotionally intelligent learning systems, AI-based instructional design, and AI literacy education. These findings indicate the quick maturity and growing educational relevance of the area, as well as the need for more diverse and rigorous research to tap into the full transformative potential of multimodal AI in education. Despite providing a full overview of this everchanging discipline, this research is constrained by both database limits and bibliometric limitations, indicating the requirement for further research in multiple databases and qualitative analysis.  © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Role of Ethical Principles and AI Characteristics in Shaping Generative AI Use in Higher Education and Its Impact on Academic Performance

Abstract: The rapid integration of Generative AI in higher education has transformed teaching and learning, yet limited research explores the factors driving its adoption and impact on academic performance. Title: Ensemble Learning for Early Academic Performance Prediction: A Case Study in Engineering Leveling Courses
Source title: Proceedings of the LACCEI international Multi-conference for Engineering, Education and Technology
Abstract: Student attrition in engineering leveling courses is a persistent challenge in Latin American higher education, often exacerbated by the lack of timely identification mechanisms. Traditional Early Warning Systems (EWS) frequently rely on midterm grades, limiting their capacity for preventive intervention. This paper presents an Ensemble Learning model designed to predict final academic performance using exclusively pre-enrollment data, combining sociodemographic, previous academic records, and socioeconomic and psychometric variables. This study analyzed historical records of 1,533 students (7,210 instances) from a polytechnic university in Ecuador. Five machine learning algorithm families were evaluated through rigorous hyperparameter optimization involving 9,972 configurations. The proposed Stacking architecture, which integrates the top-performing XGBoost models via a Ridge Regression meta-learner, achieved a Coefficient of Determination (R2) of 0.749 and a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 3.783 on a 0-40 scale, demonstrating superior generalization compared to single models. Furthermore, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis revealed that non-cognitive factors, such as study habits and academic self-confidence, are critical predictors alongside high school GPA and mathematics admission scores. To validate its practical utility, the model was deployed for the 2025-B cohort (N=900), identifying 9.2% of incoming students as "High Risk" before the start of classes. These results demonstrate the technical feasibility and ethical viability of using advanced ensemble methods for proactive, evidence-based academic management. © 2026 Latin American and Caribbean Consortium of Engineering Institutions. Title: Designing Digital Mourning: Human-Computer Interaction in AI-Generated Emotional Video
Source title: Proceedings of 2026 International Conference on Information Management and Technology, ICIMTech 2026
Abstract: The rise of generative AI in film demands a rethinking of artistic authenticity and emotional connection. This study explores audience responses to WAI Studio's Kling AI Creative Studio-produced short movie 'Paper Phone' about the culturally significant Chinese Qingming Festival. The study examines technologically sophisticated consumers' views on human-centered AI and creative tools, focusing on the psychological shift from emotional engagement to critical detachment. The mixed-methods study employed purposive sampling to acquire quantitative survey data and in-depth qualitative comments from 150 Visual Communication Design students. Data were collected before and after the video's AI-generated origins were revealed and analyzed using theme coding. The qualitative study revealed four audience positions: emotional skepticism, pragmatic optimism, visual defect examination, and creative industry danger concern. After intense emotions, the AI disclosure was a 'psychological off-switch,' causing students to focus on technical AI indications including anatomical mistakes, unreasonable physical interactions, and the 'Uncanny Valley' issue. Ethical concerns included 'soullessness' of media without human experience, 'stolen' data, and the ecological cost of AI. The research suggests that to build a strong digital environment, we need AI that values human empathy over computational simulation. Artificial intelligence is able to generate in an instant, but needs to be paired with human intention and cultural accuracy to evoke emotional resonance. These findings contribute to HCI theory by demonstrating the fragility of human-AI emotional bonds in delicate contexts such as digital mourning. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: HISE-KT: Synergizing Heterogeneous Information Networks and LLMs for Explainable Knowledge Tracing with Meta-Path Optimization
Source title: Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence
Abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) aims to mine students’ evolving knowledge states and predict their future question-answering performance. Existing methods based on heterogeneous information networks (HINs) are prone to introducing noises due to manual or random selection of meta-paths and lack necessary quality assessment of meta-path instances. Conversely, recent large language models (LLMs)-based methods ignore the rich information across students, and both paradigms struggle to deliver consistently accurate and evidence-based explanations. To address these issues, we propose an innovative framework, HIN-LLM Synergistic Enhanced Knowledge Tracing (HISE-KT), which seam-lessly integrates HINs with LLMs. HISE-KT first builds a multi-relationship HIN containing diverse node types to capture the structural relations through multiple meta-paths. The LLM is then employed to intelligently score and filter meta-path instances and retain high-quality paths, pioneering automated meta-path quality assessment. Inspired by educational psychology principles, a similar student retrieval mechanism based on meta-paths is designed to provide a more valuable context for prediction. Finally, HISE-KT uses a structured prompt to integrate the target student’s history with the retrieved similar trajectories, enabling the LLM to generate not only accurate predictions but also evidence-backed, explainable analysis reports. Experiments on four public datasets show that HISE-KT outperforms existing KT baselines in both prediction performance and interpretability. © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). Title: Reframing artificial intelligence and learning analytics in emerging higher education: towards a human-centred and contextually responsive future
Source title: Frontiers in Education
Abstract: Introduction – Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics (LA) are increasingly used to enhance student outcomes and support institutional decision-making in higher education. However, evidence from emerging economies remains fragmented and unevenly distributed across regions. This critical scoping review synthesises current evidence on AI and LA implementation across higher education institutions in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, and the Middle East. Methods – The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute Population-Concept-Context (PCC) framework and was reported in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Systematic searches of eight academic databases and selected grey literature sources identified 31 eligible publications published between 2019 and 2026. The evidence base comprised 20 empirical studies, 6 conceptual papers, and 5 policy or grey literature sources. To enhance transparency, studies were classified using a structured evidence-grading framework ranging from Grade A (high evidence) to Grade D (conceptual and policy evidence). Results – Four dominant application areas emerged: predictive early-warning systems, adaptive learning platforms, generative AI tools, and institutional analytics dashboards. Considerable regional variation was identified. Latin America demonstrated comparatively greater implementation maturity, while Sub-Saharan Africa placed greater emphasis on governance, ethics, and data justice. South Asia showed strong technical sophistication but limited pedagogical integration, whereas evidence from the Middle East reflected predominantly early-stage implementation. Across all regions, evaluation focused primarily on technical performance, with comparatively limited attention given to educational impact, equity outcomes, and long-term sustainability. Through a three-stage analytical synthesis, the review develops the Human-Centred AI and Learning Analytics Implementation Framework (HCAI-LIF), comprising four interdependent dimensions: Governance, Pedagogy, Equity, and Sustainability. Discussion – The review reframes AI and LA as socio-technical systems that require context-sensitive adaptation and responsible implementation rather than technology-driven adoption alone. The proposed framework provides an evidence-informed foundation for policymakers, institutional leaders, and researchers seeking to promote equitable, sustainable, and human-centred digital transformation in higher education across emerging economies. © 2026 Alenezi.

Title: Adoption rates and knowledge of generative artificial intelligence in pharmacy practice: A comparative study in an internet-restricted country
Source title: Digital Health
Abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping healthcare, including pharmacy practice through drug interaction screening or treatment monitoring applications. In internet-restricted settings such as Syria, access to most AI-based platforms and digital tools is limited, which may hinder their adoption in community pharmacy practice. However, adoption of AI in such contexts remains largely unexplored. Objective: To evaluate the level of AI adoption among community pharmacists in Syria and compare their familiarity and openness toward AI technologies with that of pharmacy students. Methods: A total of 400 participants based in Syria were included: 200 community pharmacists and 200 pharmacy students. Data were collected through a combination of paper-based surveys (pharmacists) and online questionnaires (students). To enhance understanding, a five-slide presentation explaining basic AI concepts was made available to participants unfamiliar with the topic. Results: Nearly half of respondents (55%; n = 219) reported using AI tools in daily life, with ChatGPT being the most recognized (53%, n = 211). Pharmacists demonstrated higher AI knowledge than students (5.7% vs. 2.5%; χ2 (4, N = 400) = 19.39, p = .001). However, students showed significantly greater willingness toward integrating AI into future practice (χ2 (2, N = 396) = 33.35, p < .001). Pharmacists with either less than two years or more than six years of experience were less likely to use AI, whereas those with limited prior Generative AI knowledge appeared more willing to adopt such tools compared with those with higher prior knowledge (OR = 9.0, 95% CI [1.36–59.78], p = .023). Conclusion: Our findings revealed a clear coexistence of interest in and concern about AI among both community pharmacists and pharmacy students. The study underscores the importance of developing clear regulatory guidance, structured training, and context-appropriate oversight to ensure the safe integration of AI into pharmacy practice, particularly in internet-restricted settings. © The Author(s) 2026. Title: Mapping fifty years of technology-enhanced science and mathematics education in Computers & Education: Trends and connections with technologies, functions, and theories
Source title: Computers and Education
Abstract: This study reviewed 50 years of research on technology-enhanced science and mathematics education published in Computers & Education (1976–2026). Following PRISMA 2020 framework, 519 empirical studies were identified. BERTopic-based topic modeling was applied to derive the thematic structure of the corpus, and each article was coded for education level, theoretical framework, primary technology, and technology function. Seventeen topics were identified, including ten science-related, four mathematics-related, and three domain-general ones. Topic membership was more strongly associated with primary technology and technology function than with education level and theoretical framework. Game-based learning split into separate science and mathematics topics, and a mathematics-centered AI/agent topic emerged, while AI-related science studies were found to be mainly assigned to existing topics such as argumentation, collaborative learning, and inquiry. VR was a distinct technological topic and served several instructional functions. Besides, research within this corpus shifted from computer-centered instructional agendas toward a more diverse space encompassing learning analytics, games, mobile and immersive environments, eye tracking, and AI, with integrated STEM and eye-tracking topics emerging in this corpus around the mid-2010s. Science-related work differentiated around disciplinary practices, whereas mathematics-related work clustered around forms of instructional support rather than mathematical subdomains. Future work can extend the BERTopic framework to a broader set of journals to fully understand the overall trends, or apply BERTopic method separately to publications within fixed intervals to examine how research topics evolve over time. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Can Students Tell, and Does It Matter? Detecting, Evaluating, and Calibrating Instructor AI Use in the Marketing Classroom
Source title: Journal of Marketing Education
Abstract: Marketing classrooms model the professional use of generative artificial intelligence (AI), but instructor AI use also creates an educational service encounter in which students judge trust, effort, and the performance of the instructor role. Using parallel surveys from 340 students and seven instructors across 10 sections of Principles of Marketing, this study examines whether students detect instructor AI use, how they evaluate it by task and agent, and whether instructors anticipate those evaluations. Students were weak detectors: estimates of AI-generated or AI-assisted course content corresponded only modestly with instructor benchmarks and varied more within sections than between them. Detection confidence was unrelated to accuracy. At the same time, students drew meaningful evaluative boundaries. They rated AI use as more appropriate for creating materials than for grading or feedback, and rated AI below human and publisher alternatives in every task. Perceived disclosure was unrelated to trust, but perceived effort was closely associated with trust, instructor ratings, and perceived learning. Instructors viewed instructor AI use more favorably than students did and valued disclosure less. The results suggest that AI governance in marketing education should be task-specific, relationally aware, and informed by student data rather than by assumptions of student detection or instructor calibration. © The Author(s) 2026

Abstract: This The increasing adoption of AI-powered assistants such as ChatGPT in higher education has reshaped how students perform academic tasks, creating a growing need to understand the behavioral factors that drive satisfaction and continued use. Title: Analyzing Educational Video Transcripts with LLMs: Accuracy, Named Entities, and Interpretability

Abstract: Digital educational media platforms such as YouTube are increasingly used by teachers and learners, creating a growing record of instructional discourse. For educational data mining (EDM) and learning analytics researchers, transcript-derived text offers a scalable entry point for corpus-level analysis, but automatically generated transcripts can contain errors that disproportionately affect named entities and downstream applications. The results reveal an important task-dependent trade-off: spaCy performed best at general entity detection, whereas GPT-5.5 showed stronger aggregate performance for codebook-constrained entity typing on gold-entity rows. Across the full corpus, PERSON, GPE, and NORP were the most frequent model-coded categories. Topic modeling comparisons further show that transcript-conditioning choices can change thematic separation and interpretability. Together, the findings demonstrate why transcript quality and entity validity should be evaluated according to the downstream educational research task. Title: A Review of AI-Powered Personalized Language Learning: Implications for Vocabulary Acquisition in L2 Learners
Source title: International Journal of Humanities Education
Abstract: This systematic review examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in personalizing vocabulary acquisition for second language (L2) learners. Following PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines, thirty-one peer-reviewed empirical studies (2020–2025) were identified across six academic databases and analyzed using a standardized six-category coding template. The review addresses three research questions: (1) the types of AI personalization techniques employed, (2) the learner data used to drive adaptivity, and (3) the effectiveness of these approaches across diverse learner profiles. Thematic and quantitative coding identified nine personalization technique categories, with adaptive learning systems predominating (32.3%), followed by chatbot/conversational AI and natural language processing (NLP)-based feedback (16.1% each). Performance metrics were the most frequently leveraged data type (54.8%), while affective and cognitive load indicators remained substantially underutilized. Findings confirm that AI personalization enhances short-term vocabulary retention and motivation—with statistically significant gains reported across key studies—though effectiveness is contingent on proficiency level, task type, and cognitive load management. Critically, 54.8% of studies reported no standardized effect sizes, and 67.7% targeted university-level learners exclusively. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory, Input Processing Theory, and the Noticing Hypothesis, the review calls for theoretically anchored, methodologically rigorous, and demographically diversified research to advance learner-centered AI design in L2 education. © 2026 Common Ground Research Networks. Title: Drone-based Estimation of Chlorophyll-A in Reservoirs: A Cubist-based Ensemble Model
Source title: 3rd International Conference on Unmanned Vehicle Systems-Oman: Intelligent Systems for Industrial Challenges, UVS 2026
Abstract: Water quality monitoring is crucial for optimal reservoir operation and management. chlorophyll-A is a vital water quality parameter, as it plays a key role in the eutrophication of lakes and reservoirs. In this research, drone imagery and machine learning models were used to estimate chlorophyll-A concentrations in the Wadi Dayqah reservoir in Oman. Six bands from the drone's camera were used to evaluate three vegetation indices and two band ratios. The minimum-Redundancy-Maximum-Relevance (mRMR) algorithm was utilized to identify the most influential features for chlorophyll-A estimation. These features include thermal band, blue band, Normalized Difference Red Edge index (NDREi), Green Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (GNDVI), and the blue-To-green ratio. The Lazy Predict library was utilized to fit 42 regression models and to sort them based on their predictive performance. Four of the best-performing models, namely, Extra Trees, LightGBM, NuSVR, and AdaBoost regressors, were selected. After hyperparameter tuning, they achieved a coefficient of determination (R2) of 0.70,0.68,0.67, and 0.67, respectively. These models were used as base-learners for the ensemble Cubist meta-learner model, which enhanced the R2 score to 0.82. The results show the effectiveness of coupling Lazy Predict with the Cubist model to improve chlorophyll-A prediction accuracy in reservoirs.  © 2026 IEEE.

Abstract: Nowadays, the adult learners experience the problems in their lifelong learning process such as the lack of competence in the use of digital tools, poor adaptability to intelligent technologies, and poor effectiveness of learning transfer, impeding the process of further enhancement of their digital literacy. Title: Enhancing Learning Design Workflows with Generative AI using Navigation Support

Abstract: Learning Analytics (LA) stands as a core pillar in leveraging generative AI for smart learning environments, yet its full potential is notably hindered by critical shortcomings in current AI-assisted Learning Design (LD) tools. Title: Explaining Student Performance Prediction and Generating Personalized Actionable Feedback Using Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) with SHAP
Source title: Lecture Notes in Computer Science
Abstract: Effective student performance prediction enables timely support in Educational Data Mining (EDM). However, most predictive models lack interpretability and do not provide actionable feedback for learners. To address prediction accuracy and explanation, this study integrates an optimized XGBoost classifier with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD), our model employs SMOTE-based class balancing and randomized hyperparameter tuning, achieving better performance than existing research. To address the challenge that predictive models typically function as black boxes without providing concrete guidance for instructors and students, SHAP explanations generate individualized reports that highlight the most influential features for each student’s predicted outcome. These explanations are mapped to targeted, prioritized feedback aligned with students’ learning needs. Case studies demonstrate how the system offers concrete and interpretable guidance for both at-risk and high-performing students. This study addresses a key EDM gap by moving beyond prediction to support personalized intervention. Title: A Novel Hybrid Empirical Discrete Metaheuristic and Simplex Algorithm With Branch Separation for Optimal Photovoltaic Allocation in Radial Distribution Networks

Abstract: Optimal placement and sizing of photovoltaic (PV) plants in radial distribution networks remains challenging due to the trade-off between global search and local precision. This paper proposes a hybrid algorithm that combines a modified empirical discrete metaheuristic (EDM), the simplex complex method, and a novel branch separation division (DSR) strategy. Title: Can theory-driven learning analytics dashboard enhance human-AI collaboration in writing learning? Insights from an empirical experiment
Source title: Internet and Higher Education
Abstract: The integration of Generative AI (GenAI) into education has raised concerns about over-reliance and superficial learning, particularly in writing tasks in higher education. This study explores whether a theory-driven learning analytics dashboard (LAD) can enhance human-AI collaboration in the academic writing task by improving writing knowledge gains, fostering self-regulated learning (SRL) skills and shaping different human-AI dialogue characteristics. Grounded in Zimmerman's SRL framework, the LAD provided real-time feedback on learners' goal-setting, writing processes and reflection, while monitoring the quality of learner-AI interactions. A quasi-experiment was conducted involving 52 postgraduate students in a human-AI collaborative writing task. The students were divided into an experimental group (EG) that used the LAD and a control group (CG) that did not. Pre- and post- knowledge tests, questionnaires measuring SRL and cognitive load, and students' dialogue data with GenAI were collected and analyzed. Results showed that the EG achieved significantly higher writing knowledge gains and improved SRL skills, particularly in self-efficacy and cognitive strategies. However, the EG also reported increased test anxiety and cognitive load, possibly due to heightened metacognitive awareness. Epistemic Network Analysis revealed that the EG engaged in more reflective, evaluative interactions with GenAI, while the CG focused on more transactional and information-seeking exchanges. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on the educational use of GenAI and highlight the importance of designing interventions that complement GenAI tools, ensuring that technology enhances rather than undermines the learning process. © 2025 Elsevier Inc.

Title: How does artificial intelligence compare to human feedback? A meta-analysis of performance, feedback perception, and learning dispositions
Source title: Educational Psychology
Abstract: This exploratory meta-analysis synthesises current research on the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-generated feedback compared to traditional human-provided feedback. Drawing on 41 studies involving a total of 4813 students, the findings reveal no statistically significant differences in learning performance between students who received AI-generated feedback and those who received human-provided feedback. The pooled effect size was small and statistically insignificant (Hedge’s g = 0.25, CI [−0.11; 0.60]), indicating that AI feedback is potentially as effective as human feedback. A separate meta-analysis focusing exclusively on studies in the domain of language and writing confirmed similar findings, with high heterogeneity persisting (I2 = 95%). The study further explored differences in feedback perception and found a small, negative, and statistically insignificant effect size (Hedge’s g = −0.20, CI [−0.67; 0.27]). The study advocates for a hybrid approach, leveraging the scalability of AI while retaining the deep, empathetic, and contextual features of human feedback. © 2025 The Author(s). Title: BLADE-LA: A Bi-LSTM Attention-Driven Graph-Enhanced Framework for Student Mastery Prediction

Abstract: In this paper, we introduce BLADE-LA (Bi-LSTM Attention-Driven Graph-Enhanced Learning Analytics), a deep learning framework that combines bidirectional long short term memory networks, multi-head attention mechanism and graph convolutional networks to predict the degree of mastery as well as risk status of students in adaptive learning environments. The proposed model takes as input multi-modal student interaction data-such as clickstream logs, assessment responses, engagement time-series and contextual meta-data-and passes them through a temporal encoding step using Bi-LSTM followed by an attention-weighted contextualization step followed by a graph-based reasoning stage that makes use of a dynamically constructed knowledge-skill dependency graph. Title: A Review of Integrated Systems for Student Performance Prediction and Secure Attendance Verification

This paper conducts a structured survey of two critical, yet frequently siloed, research domains: (1) machine learning for student performance prediction and (2) secure, automated attendance systems. Our review traces the evolution of predictive models from traditional classifiers to high-accuracy ensemble methods like Random Forest and XGBoost, noting the parallel rise of eXplainable AI (XAI) to ensure stakeholder trust. We conclude by proposing a conceptual framework for a unified system that feeds high-integrity, verified attendance data directly into an XAI-driven predictive engine. Title: Learning Analytics Through Generative AI: An Exploratory Study
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has opened new pathways for enhancing educational technologies, particularly through the integration of learning analytics (LA). This paper explores the dynamic relationship between LA and GAI, assessing how their convergence could potentially transform educational outcomes. LA, which involves the measurement, collection, analysis, and reporting of data about learners and their contexts, serves as a crucial tool for understanding and improving learning processes. Combined with GAI, capable of creating content, simulating educational interactions, and generating personalized learning resources, the potential for tailored educational experiences is significantly expanded. This synergy not only enhances adaptive learning environments but also supports real-time decision-making, feedback, and intervention strategies. By examining various case studies and experimental implementations, the study highlights the efficacy of GAI in interpreting complex datasets provided by LA, thereby promoting an adaptive and responsive learning ecosystem. Additionally, ethical considerations, challenges, and future directions of this interdisciplinary approach are discussed to guide current and future applications. This paper proposes an exploratory study on the synergy between LA and GAI, using the AI4Design system, a web-based platform based on GAI for Design learning, as the framework where GAI complements LA. A case study is proposed using ChatGPT as the GAI engine. The first results show the power of the synergy GAI-LA. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2026.

Title: Analytics Education: Conceptual Network Structure, Key Challenges and Opportunities
Source title: IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology
Abstract: Analytic Education utilises data analysis techniques to improve educational practices and outcomes, focusing on extracting insights from educational big data and learning analytics. There has been an increasing density of research in the scientific field in this area, highlighted through bibliometric approaches. This article aims to investigate emerging research trends in Analytic Education and the opportunities for adopting data analysis in higher education, promoting predictive analyses to foster evidence-based practices that can transform education. The research was conducted in two main phases: a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) limited to the Scopus and Web of Science databases, covering the period from 2020 to 2024, to identify and evaluate evidence in the literature, followed by a meta-analysis using term association in SciMAT to map research topics and collaborations. The study observed a substantial increase in publications on analytic education starting in 2023, identifying topics such as “Data Analytics,” “Higher Education,” and “Predictive Analytics” as emerging areas. A strong initial connection exists between big educational data and learning analytics, expanding to integrate artificial intelligence and adaptive learning systems. This points to an integrated approach that is considered fundamental in analytic education. In contrast, big educational data highlights the expansion of educational possibilities. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2026.

Title: Large Language Models and NLP in Learning Management Systems: A Systematic Review of Dropout Interventions
Source title: Lecture Notes in Educational Technology
Abstract: Recent advances in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have significantly enhanced text analysis and generation capabilities, introducing new tools that may help reduce student dropout rates. Concurrently, the growing adoption of Learning Management Systems (LMS) has contributed to an increase in educational data volume, creating opportunities for intervention through learning analytics applications. In this context, this study conducts a systematic review of research published over the past decade to investigate how NLP has been used to identify or mitigate the risk of student dropout in LMS such as Moodle and Canvas LMS. A search was performed across the Scopus and Web of Science databases, yielding a total of 142 results. After applying inclusion and exclusion criteria, 19 studies employing diverse approaches were selected and analyzed. Although relevant applications have been proposed, the results suggest that few studies provide data demonstrating the efficacy of such interventions, underscoring the need for further evidence to guide the implementation of NLP in these environments. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2026.

Authors: Vasuki D.P.; Bharath S.; Kumar D.S.; Sagar V.K.
Title: Adaptive Context-Aware RAG Engine Via Multiple Task Semi-Supervised Self-Paced Learning.
Source title: International Conference on Computational Robotics, Testing and Engineering Evaluation, ICCRTEE 2026
Abstract: Modern educational frameworks desperately need personalized tutoring and dynamic cognitive routing. In this research work introduces an adaptive context aware retrieval augmented generation (RAG) Engine a cutting-edge AI framework designed to generate hallucination-free academic content and real-time student evaluations. To guarantee instant performance and absolute factual accuracy, we integrated Llama 3.1 and optimized FAISS vector indexing, executing the entire pipeline on ultra-fast Groq LPUs. The core of our architecture is an Educational Knowledge Tracing (EKT) system driven by a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, which tracks temporal learning patterns across varying cognitive complexities. This research work is primarily designed for robust integration into smart educational platforms as an autonomous, self-paced AI tutor. By merging Multi-Task, Semi-Supervised, and Self-Paced Learning methodologies, the system actively reads a student's cognitive load and dynamically shifts its teaching method to match their exact proficiency level. We evaluated the system using strict parameters, including predictive accuracy, Area Under Curve (AUC), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), and generative latency. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed NEXUS EKT framework. It significantly outperforms traditional knowledge tracing baselines by achieving a 93.2% accuracy rate, eventually enabling faster, more precise, and highly personalized educational interventions. ©2026 IEEE.

Title: Sustainability-Aware Learning-Analytics-Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented AI Tutor for Inclusive Higher Education in Resource-Constrained Settings
Source title: 2026 6th International Conference on Intelligent Communications and Computing, ICICC 2026
Abstract: Generative AI tutors can broaden access to academic support, but unconstrained advice can be ungrounded, unfair, and costly for institutions with limited resources. This paper presents a sustainability-aware framework that combines early learning analytics with retrieval-augmented feedback for inclusive higher education. Using the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset, we predict at-risk learners from the first 28 days of activity and then retrieve course statistics, assessment evidence, and support policies to produce traceable feedback. In a reproducible experiment over 32593 student-course records, the best early-risk model, Random Forest, achieved Macro-F1=0.764, AUC =0.846, and at-risk recall =0.679. The feedback audit shows that grounded feedback reached evidence coverage of 1.00 and unsupported-claim rate of 0. 0 0, compared with 1. 0 0 for generic non-retrieval advice. The results support a compact, auditable AI tutor design aligned with SDG 4 quality education and SDG 10 reduced inequalities, without claiming real classroom learning gains. © 2026 IEEE.

Title: Assessment and Feedback Through Generative AI Intelligent Tutoring Systems
Source title: Collaborative Paradigms of Generative AI and Human Intelligence for Equitable Learning Futures
Abstract: This chapter explores how Generative AI (GenAI) is transforming assessment and feedback in education through Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS). As learning shifts toward more personalized, inclusive, and data-driven approaches, GenAI enables real-time adaptive feedback, conversational learning, and dynamic assessment tailored to individual needs. It examines the integration of GenAI technologies—like natural language processing—into ITS architectures to create personalized, context-aware evaluations. Ethical concerns such as bias, transparency, and inclusion are addressed, emphasizing the need for human-AI collaboration. Case studies from K–12, higher education, and vocational training highlight practical applications. The chapter also discusses how GenAI, supported by learning analytics and formative assessment, can move evaluation beyond summative tests toward continuous, learner-centered progress tracking. Ultimately, GenAI is presented as a powerful tool for deeper learning and meaningful feedback—provided it is developed responsibly and with strong educator engagement. Author full names: Tateiwa, Yuichiro (24924007100); Chen, Guoyi (60740037700); Luo, Zhaonan (60739950500); Uchiya, Takahiro (6602953088); Yin, Chengjiu (56054510500)
Title: Learning Strategies and Learning Outcomes in Virtual Network Exercises: An Integrated Analysis of E-Textbook, Exercise Operations, and Web Usage Logs
Source title: 2026 22nd International Conference on Information Technology Based Higher Education and Training, ITHET 2026
Abstract: Understanding learner behavior in virtual exercise environments is essential for improving practical computing education. This study investigated the relationship between observable learning behaviors and learning outcomes in a university-level network security exercise course. A total of 28,284 log events were collected from three complementary data sources - an e-textbook system, a virtual network exercise platform, and web access records via a browser extension - as nine learners worked through 22 mandatory tasks. E-textbook browsing patterns were classified into three categories (SEEK, ZAP, DEEP) based on dwell time, and analyzed alongside terminal and GUI operations in the exercise system. The analysis revealed a counterintuitive "deep-reading paradox": a strong association was found between a higher proportion of DEEP browsing on reference pages and a higher low-score rate. This suggests that prolonged dwell time on pages may reflect learning stagnation rather than genuine deep understanding. In contrast, high scorers executed significantly more HALT-initiated stop-modify-restart cycles in the exercise environment (3.87 times more than low scorers), and the quality of post-error responses - rather than sheer command volume - were associated with differences in learning outcomes. No significant association was found between web search frequency and learning outcomes, and an exploratory analysis of generative AI usage suggested a negative trend that was not statistically significant. Integrating these results, we summarize the behavioral patterns characteristic of high scorers. Early broad exploration was associated with final grades, especially among high scorers, and throughout the entire period, high scorers tended to engage in structured trial-and-error and selective use of learning materials. We also discuss practical implications regarding early intervention and explicit instruction of trial-and-error strategies.  © 2026 IEEE.

Authors: Tzimas D.E.; Demetriadis S.N.
Author full names: Tzimas, Dimitrios E. (57222294957); Demetriadis, Stavros N. (6506681303)
Title: Implementing Learning Analytics in Education: Enhancing Actionability and Adoption
Source title: Computers
Abstract: The broader aim of this research is to examine how Learning Analytics (LA) can become ethically sound, pedagogically actionable, and realistically adopted in educational practice. To address this overarching challenge, the study investigates three interrelated research questions: ethics by design, learning impact, and adoption conditions. Methodologically, the research follows an exploratory sequential multi-method design. First, a meta-synthesis of 53 studies is conducted to identify key ethical challenges in LA and to derive an ethics-by-design framework. Second, a quasi-experimental study examines the impact of interface-based LA guidance (strong versus minimal) on students’ self-regulated learning skills and academic performance. Third, a mixed-methods adoption study, combining surveys, focus groups, and ethnographic observations, investigates the factors that encourage or hinder teachers’ adoption of LA in K–12 education. The findings indicate that strong LA-based guidance leads to statistically significant improvements in students’ self-regulated learning skills and academic performance compared to minimal guidance. Furthermore, the adoption analysis reveals that performance expectancy, social influence, human-centred design, and positive emotions facilitate LA adoption, whereas effort expectancy, limited facilitating conditions, ethical concerns, and cultural resistance inhibit it. Overall, the study demonstrates that ethics by design, effective pedagogical guidance, and adoption conditions are mutually reinforcing dimensions. It argues that LA can support intelligent, responsive, and human-centred learning environments when ethical safeguards, instructional design, and stakeholder involvement are systematically aligned. © 2026 by the authors.

Authors: Duan Z.; Shi Z.; Jia B.; Wang Q.
Title: MicroC-KT: Modeling Community Effect via Learning Micro-Environment for Evidence-Grounded Explainable Knowledge Tracing
Source title: Proceedings of the Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
Abstract: Knowledge Tracing (KT) is essential for tracking students' evolving knowledge states and predicting their future performance. While current graph-based methods focus on exercise-concept relations, they often overlook the inherent group structures among students. Similarly, emerging LLM-based approaches rely on individual histories, lacking the broader context of group references and contrastive evidence. As a result, existing individual-isolation paradigms fail to provide stable predictions and evidence-based explanations. To bridge this gap, we propose Micro-Community Knowledge Tracing (MicroC-KT), a framework that incorporates learning micro-environments to provide social-cognitive anchors for KT. MicroC-KT identifies latent learning communities via hypergraph modeling and generates dual-granular summaries to facilitate community matching and peer retrieval. By extracting contrastive group evidence, the model prompts an LLM to generate both accurate answer predictions and verifiable analysis reports. Experiments on four public datasets demonstrate that MicroC-KT significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in predictive performance while providing more reliable and evidence-based explanations. © 2026 Association for Computational Linguistics.

Title: The role of evidence-based data and analytics in medical education management
Source title: Cogent Education
Abstract: In the context of digitalization in education and increasing demands for evidence-based decision-making, the tools of educational analytics have gained particular importance. This study investigated the influence of academic data, visualized through Power BI, on managerial decisions. The unit of analysis comprised educational programs, with aggregated data on student performance metrics across three levels of training: undergraduate, internship, and residency. The sample included approximately 1,900 students from the NAO ‘Astana Medical University’ (Kazakhstan). A study was conducted integrating quantitative analysis of academic performance with a qualitative examination of managerial decision-making related to educational programs. Data sources included Power BI analytical dashboards, administrative documentation, and semi-structured interviews with university administrators (n = 6). The objective was to trace the relationship between academic metrics and managerial interventions. The results demonstrated positive trends: the proportion of students with unsatisfactory grades decreased from 6.76% (2024) to 1.27% (2025), while the share of high-achieving students increased from 26.14% to 29.54%. The most effective departments were those with an established culture of data-driven decision-making. Managerial measures included curriculum revisions, adjustments to teaching workloads, and personnel-related decisions. Educational analytics serves not only as a technical tool but also as a social mechanism for transforming institutional practices. Power BI functions not merely as a monitoring instrument but as an autonomous agent within managerial discourse, initiating shifts in the logic of educational design. Prospective research directions include analyzing institutional resistance to analytical practices and examining the readiness of administrators for data-driven decision-making. © 2026 The Author(s). Author full names: Hoda, Syed Rafiq ul (61012198300); Atwell, Eric (26631780000); Baig, Mirza Mahmood (61011593000)
Title: An AI-interpretable multidimensional intelligence-driven framework for student performance prediction using local LLM-based narrative reasoning
Source title: Intelligent Data Analysis
Abstract: Predicting student performance has become a vital objective in educational data mining, however existing models remain limited by limited feature sets, opaque decision processes, and the absence of real-time, context-aware interpretative intelligence. This study presents a novel hybrid Artificial Intelligence (AI) architecture that integrates cognitive, emotional, and general intelligence indicators with formative assessment/class performance data to construct a multidimensional demonstration of student performance. The system utilizes a mathematically formalized feature-weighting mechanism that allows domain experts to regulate the influence of key predictors prior to training, enabling a tunable and educator-configurable modeling process. Interaction between cognitive, emotional, and behavioral properties are explicitly engineered to capture complex effects often overlooked in prior research. An ensemble predictive model combining Random Forests, Gradient Boosting, and Linear Regression is used to predict student grades, with uncertainty measured through variance-based confidence intervals. The integrated system exhibited strong predictive capability, attaining high accuracy (R2=0.9014, 95% CI [0.8882, 0.9121], 10,000 bootstrap resamples) with low prediction error, confirming the stability and reliability of the ensemble model. Understanding why a model produces a particular prediction is often as important as the prediction itself. To address the interpretability gap, the system incorporates SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based global and local explanations, a counterfactual simulation engine that estimates the marginal impact of improving specific attributes, and a local generative AI layer deployed via Ollama that creates these outputs into structured, real-time narrative feedback. Running the Large Language Model (LLM) locally ensures privacy-preserving, institution-compliant interpretability while permitting interactive, student specific explanations. This integration of predictive modeling, explainability, simulation, and local generative reasoning creates a unified decision-support framework that exceeds traditional black-box approaches. Experimental assessment shows that the model not only achieves viable predictive accuracy but also provides actionable insights into feature influence, model stability, and potential intervention pathways. © The Author(s) 2026

Authors: Jiang P.; Wu X.; Wang W.; Xia Y.; Hou B.; Xu W.
Title: Towards efficient student performance prediction with tabular prior-data fitted network: a small-sample learning approach in data-scarce scenarios
Source title: PeerJ Computer Science
Abstract: Accurate prediction of student academic performance is crucial for enhancing educational outcomes and enabling personalized learning interventions. However, the limited availability of labeled data in many practical educational settings poses significant challenges for conventional machine learning models, which often require large datasets to achieve satisfactory performance and are prone to overfitting. To address this issue, we propose a novel small-sample learning framework based on the Tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN). By integrating a Transformer based architecture with Bayesian inference, TabPFN effectively leverages meta-learned priors to perform high-quality predictions without task-specific finetuning. We evaluated the approach on the Mathematics and Portuguese subsets of the UCI Student Performance dataset and on a pooled Combined dataset under small-sample conditions. Experimental results indicate that TabPFN achieved generally strong and competitive performance across the three datasets, with accuracies of 92.36, 95.49, and 94.29, respectively. However, its advantage varied across datasets and metrics, and the results should be interpreted cautiously where confidence intervals overlapped with strong baseline models. Additionally, we employ Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) to interpret model decisions, identifying key influencing factors such as prior grades (G1, G2) and prior educational experience. The findings indicate that TabPFN constitutes a promising and effective solution for educational prediction in data scarce scenarios but also provides actionable insights for instructional design and student support. Authors: Suprayogi M.N.; Suwarno
Author full names: Suprayogi, Muhamad Nanang (57195954440); Suwarno (57216266242)
Title: Artificial Intelligence in Digital Learning Design for Personalized and Adaptive Learning: A PRISMA-Based Systematic Literature Review
Source title: 2026 13th International Conference on ICT for Smart Society, ICISS 2026
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now shapes how learning experiences are designed, but the research linking digital and instructional learning design with AI, learning analytics, and personalized or adaptive learning is scattered across separate fields. This paper reports a systematic literature review (SLR) carried out under the PRISMA 2020 protocol. We examined open-access, English-language documents indexed in Scopus that together address learning design, AI or analytics, personalization or adaptivity, and an explicit framework, model, approach, or strategy. Of 86 records identified, one duplicate was removed, twelve were excluded during title and abstract screening, and ten during full-text assessment, which left 63 studies for synthesis. Thematic coding grouped these into six clusters: generative AI and large language models for instructional design (C1); adaptive and personalized learning systems and frameworks (C2); learning analytics for learning design and feedback (C3); cognitive and self-regulated learning with AI (C4); immersive and emerging technologies (C5); and reviews and meta-research (C6). The review answers two questions: which AI-based frameworks, models, approaches, and strategies are used to design digital learning (RQ1), and how those designs deliver personalization and adaptivity (RQ2). We consolidate the evidence into a conceptual AI-enhanced Digital Learning Design (AI-DLD) framework and discuss the open problems of equity, ethics, data privacy, and human oversight. © 2026 IEEE.

Authors: Wattanasirichaigoon S.
Author full names: Wattanasirichaigoon, Somkiat (6701428219)
Title: AI-Mediated Assessment of Continuing Medical Education: The Case-based Learning Intelligence Credit System (CLICS) Framework
Source title: JMIR Medical Education
Abstract: Continuing medical education (CME) and continuing professional development (CPD) systems have traditionally relied on time-based credit allocation, using participation duration as a proxy for professional learning. Although administratively simple and scalable, this model does not reliably demonstrate whether physicians have engaged in meaningful learning, improved clinical reasoning, or critically appraised evidence. The emergence of generative AI creates an opportunity to rethink how physician learning is documented, assessed, and credited. This viewpoint proposes the Case-based Learning Intelligence Credit System (CLICS), a conceptual framework for translating AI-mediated clinical learning interactions into auditable evidence of reasoning-related engagement that could support CME/CPD credit. CLICS introduces the professional learning episode (PLE) as the basic unit of creditable learning: a coherent AI-mediated interaction demonstrating a clinically meaningful problem, reasoning development through iterative inquiry, contextual or evidentiary integration, and reflective synthesis. PLEs are evaluated using the proposed Practice Intelligence Score-7 (PIS-7) rubric, subject to human calibration and oversight; the rubric assesses observable reasoning behavior within the episode rather than the AI’s answer, and qualifying PLEs may be translated into CME/CPD credit through threshold-based, human-auditable conversion rules. CLICS is not intended to replace traditional CME but to extend it as an optional, evidence-generating pathway for personalized, practice-embedded professional development. Its implementation requires iterative validation, stratified human audit, privacy-by-design architecture, antigaming controls, bias monitoring, and professional oversight. If validated, CLICS may enable identification of domain-specific areas for improvement and support personalized, adaptive learning pathways. © Somkiat Wattanasirichaigoon.

Authors: Ma X.; Li C.; Xu J.; Zhu S.; Li Y.
Title: Exploring characteristics of primary school students’ self-regulated learning (SRL) behaviors in human-GenAI collaborative programming learning environments: Insights from a proposed framework
Source title: Computers and Education
Abstract: Programming education in primary school is vital for nurturing future-ready talents, yet primary school students often struggle with self-regulated learning (SRL), particularly in resource utilization and strategy regulation. Although human-generative AI (GenAI) collaborative programming learning might have the potential to enhance personalized programming education, GenAI's interplay with SRL processes remains underexplored. To address this gap, this study first proposed a SRL Behavior Analysis Framework for human-GenAI collaborative programming learning environments and then examined SRL behaviors of a group of sixth-grade students (n = 36) in such an environment using this framework, along with various learning analytics methods including cluster analysis, descriptive statistics and lag sequential analysis. The analysis yielded the following results: (1) Based on their learning performance, primary school students were identified as three distinct clusters: programming specialized unit (PSU), high performance unit (HPU), and low performance unit (LPU). (2) Regarding SRL behaviors, students prioritized self-control (65.8 %), followed by self-observation (19 %), task analysis (12.1 %), and behavior stagnation (3.2 %). (3) Students in PSU and HPU consistently adopted goal-oriented SRL strategies, whereas students in LPU exhibited passive dependence and fragmented strategy use. GenAI's facilitative effect in supporting learning correlated with users' SRL capabilities. (4) Students in PSU and HPU exhibited frequent transitions between SRL behaviors, whereas students in LPU had insufficient ability to switch strategies when facing programming difficulties. Based on these findings, this study proposed four forward-looking design recommendations: effectively integrating GenAI with the programming environment, utilizing multimodal data and AI for learning assessment and feedback, building a cluster-driven early warning mechanism, and conducting dynamic SRL analysis and guidance based on fine-grained time-series data. © 2025 Elsevier Ltd

Title: GenAI as Semantic Sensors for Collaborative Learning
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping Multimodal Learning Analytics (MMLA) by augmenting and extending the semantics of learning interactions. While recent systematic research indicates that GenAI is currently used primarily for individual learners’ tasks such as tutoring or co-programming, its application in collaborative learning environments remains largely underdeveloped and overlooked. This half-day workshop invites researchers to explore how Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal generative learning and teaching architectures can serve as additional sources of semantic sensors to decode meaning, motivation, coherence, and learning performance in group learning. Title: Validating AI-Simulated Students for Early Regression Testing of Adaptive Learning Controllers

Abstract: Adaptive learning systems are difficult to test during development because live studies are slow, costly, and ethically non-trivial, creating a practical "cold-start"whenever a new controller or policy is introduced. Title: Temporal Meta Learning Framework for Early Student at Risk Prediction in Online Learning Environments

Abstract: The need for trustworthy early warning systems that can spot students at academic risk before disengagement results in course failure or withdrawal has increased due to the quick expansion of online learning settings. The Open University Learning Analytics dataset, which includes 32,593 anonymized student records with failed and withdrew students classified as at risk, is used to assess the model. To guarantee a fair assessment of predictive performance, a thorough evaluation approach is used, utilizing accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score, and area under the receiver furthermore characteristic curve. Experimental results show that the proposed model achieves an AUC ROC score of 0.8893, an F1 score of 0.8028, a precision of 0.8990, and a recall of 0.7251, indicating strong discrimination capability with high confidence predictions. Comparative analysis against logistic regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, and LightGBM demonstrates that while ensemble methods yield higher recall, the proposed temporal framework provides superior precision by effectively capturing sequential engagement patterns. Title: AI Integration in Indonesian Education: Trends, Outcomes, and Challenges - A Comprehensive Review

Abstract: Background: Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method: Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results: The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion: These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation. Title: Modeling Time-Sensitive Causal Uplift in Marketing Campaigns: Evidence From Synthetic and Real-World Data

Abstract: Uplift modeling (or incremental response modeling) is a technique used in many business applications to estimate the causal impact of an intervention. In the potential outcomes approach, it has established a conceptual basis for marketing analytics and causal inference studies, enabling more effective targeting of customers whose behavior is affected. Rather than focusing only on who is likely to respond, it looks at why and when responses occur. The approach estimates individualized treatment effects (ITEs) to identify which customers react specifically because of a marketing intervention. The analysis proceeds in two stages. First, a controlled synthetic dataset is designed to simulate real-world variation in demographics, behavior, and treatment assignment bias. Title: HPrEd: A Tuned Ensemble With Model-Agnostic XAI to Explain Social Media’s Association With Academic Productivity
Source title: IEEE Access
Abstract: Social media plays a crucial role in shaping students’ academic productivity, both as an effective learning tool and as a source of confusion. However, most studies are limited to basic statistical analysis or a single machine learning model, which often lacks structured evaluation and interpretability. Such methods typically perform poorly on heterogeneous datasets and fail to provide sufficient insights for practical applications. To overcome these limitations, this study proposes a soft voting ensemble called Hybrid Productivity Prediction (HPrEd), which combines multiple machine learning (ML) models. Model-agnostic explainable AI (XAI) techniques LIME and SHAP are used to analyze the relationship between social media engagement and academic productivity. SMOTE is applied to reduce class asymmetry and RFE is used to select the best features. To select the appropriate model for HPrEd, a systematic comparison was made between three ML model families: tree-based, distance-based, and neural network-based, where Extra Trees, k-NN, and MLP were combined based on their complementary strengths. The robustness of the model was verified through 5-fold cross-validation. HPrEd achieved the highest recall of 98.25% and only 0.53% false alarm probability (PF). SHAP analysis showed that delay in starting studies, decreased attention to academic work, increased coursework distraction, and perceived productivity in the absence of social media were the most influential factors, with normalized SHAP values ranging from −1.2×10−16 to +1.6×10−16. Additionally, the LIME-based local interpretation found that moderate levels of multitasking during study (0.62), significant feelings of time loss (1.59), high self-reported academic impact (1.67), and low ability to limit social media use (45) had the greatest impact on individual predictors, with class probability exceeding 99%. Overall, the results suggest that excessive social media use is associated with decreased academic productivity, but moderate levels of use may be helpful in increasing attention in some cases. These insights provide guidance for educators and policymakers and support future longitudinal research. © 2026 The Authors.
